subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DIRECTIVE ON JOB
subsubtopic: PLACEMENT PRIORITIES REPLACING THAT OF MARCH 9-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to my statements yesterday and Tuesday I wish to tell the House the outcome of my review of the departmental directive on placement priorities, issued on March 9.
As pointed out on Tuesday, suitability for work is the overriding criterion for referral to jobs, and any directive issued must be read in the context of the Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations which govern the operation of the employment service of the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
Yesterday I indicated my understanding that the reason for issuing the directive had been related to the very specific policy announced some time ago for the local initiatives and training-on-the-job programs. In those cases unemployment insurance and welfare recipients were to be given priority in placement.
Further to the undertaking I gave to the House yesterday I have reviewed the March 9 directive with my senior officials of the department. Because its wording could be and has been misunderstood-

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW DIRECTIVE ON JOB
subsubtopic: PLACEMENT PRIORITIES REPLACING THAT OF MARCH 9-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
It reads:
This cancels and replaces my telex of March 9th.
The purpose of that telex was to emphasize the importance of aggressive, affirmative action by CMCs to utilize emerging employment opportunities, especially those created by the local initiative and training-on-the job programs for those people who are definitely unemployed and in need.
As you are aware, priority in referral to jobs is governed by Regulation 27 to the Unemployment Insurance Regulations. Consistent with Regulation 27, all job orders will be checked as soon as they are received against existing live files of registrations to ensure that preference in referral is given to qualified registrants as required by the regulation. The telex of March 9th was not intended to change this basic procedure.
In the case of the LIP and training-on-the-job programs it has been publicly announced as government policy that priority in placement would be given to those who are unemployed. Within that priority emphasis must be given to those on unemployment insurance, welfare or otherwise unemployed and actively seeking work.
A special effort must be made to complete recruitment for LIP and training-on-the-job, particularly the latter, as quickly as possible and in accordance with the foregoing policy.
Mr. Speaker, looking at Regulation 27 of the Unemployment Insurance Regulations which was written many years ago, I am advised that it could be construed so narrowly as to prohibit special action on behalf of almost any category of disadvantaged groups including youth, native workers, the handicapped, women returning to the labour force and those who have been chronically bypassed in the labour market. We are trying to do a better job for all Canadian workers, but in particular to ensure that the procedures do not inadvertently penalize certain groups. I am going to review Regulation 27 and, if necessary recommend updating it, in order to guarantee that we are permitted to help those who need help most.
In summary, while I regret the misunderstanding caused by the unfortunate wording of the earlier departmental directive, I want to indicate my strong support of the administrative objective, which was to generate a more positive and dynamic effort to put unemployed people in jobs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the minister's statement. But let me tell him, through you, Sir, that there is something that stinks around here. I can only put it that bluntly.

Mr. Speaker, what I think has happened is that the minister, in error, brought about a directive that was totally unacceptable and, having found out what had occurred, he is now trying to weasel out of that directive. The unfortunate part is that, although he mentioned the directive of last Friday by way of date, March 9, he at no time referred to it in his statement in total nor has he indicated that that directive would be laid on the table. I think this is an irresponsible attitude for him to take.
There is something else that bothers me with respect to the minister's statement. I quote from the third paragraph which begins with the words: "Yesterday I indicated my understanding". This leads us on this side of the House to think that the minister is not running his department. It appears to me, after having read certain quotes in last night's paper, that he is apologizing on behalf of the deputy minister. It is the minister himself, Mr. Speaker, who is responsible for the mess in which he has placed himself. I cannot understand how the minister can take that attitude when this matter was published in the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, March 13. That gave him ample time to understand what the problem was going to be in terms of questions in the House. He now says that he did not even see the directive. If he did not see it, I do not know why he answered the questions that were posed to him from this side of the House at such length.
I just want to refer to this matter, Mr. Speaker. On Tuesday I asked the minister the following question:
Has the minister instructed his department to give absolute priority in referrals for all jobs, including on-the-job-training, to unemployment insurance claimants in the first instance, welfare recipients in the second instance, and other unemployed persons in the third instance? If so, does this mean that the policy of the department is now one of high selectivity, seemingly ignoring suitability of skills and the needs of employers as well as of other Canadians?
From that question on, Mr. Speaker, the minister led the House to believe that he knew what we were talking about, and I respectfully suggest that he did. He knew just what was happening but when he ran into flak then came the problem.

I do not understand the minister either when in this new telex he refers to the telex of last Friday in the following words:
The purpose of that telex was to emphasize the importance of aggressive, affirmative action by CMCs to utilize emerging employment opportunities, especially those created by the local initiative and training-on-the-job programs-
Do you remember that yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the minister was emphatic in stating that this directive applied to the local initiatives program? He was emphatic in the House, and outside the House on radio, television and in the press he was emphatic again. But I notice he has now

included the training-on-the-job program. I question the minister's credibility in this regard. I also question it because the telex states "especially". When you use the word "especially" it means that it was not referred to at all before, nor was it in the minister's mind to devote this directive to LIP. I am not even happy with the telex that he has now sent out because he questions whether he is doing it in the right way because regulation 27 leads him to believe that he cannot do what he is doing right now. The minister says in his statement:
I am going to review Regulation 27 and, if necessary, recommend updating it, in order to guarantee that we are permitted to help those who need help most.
I recall that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) asked yesterday whether the minister had the approval of the Governor General in Council with respect to this directive, but he has not indicated to date whether he had that approval. He probably did not sign it. He has also indicated, Mr. Speaker, that what he is doing is wrong because he is saying, by implication, that he does not know if he can do it when he has to review Regulation 27.
I still question the directive because it is my understanding that manpower services are for the need and use of all Canadians. I think that what the minister is doing is being done because of the embarrassment of high unemployment and the high unemployment insurance costs. It is being done for the benefit of the Liberal party to the exclusion and disadvantage of the people of Canada. Manpower services are to be used without selectivity to any great extent, if at all, nor are they to be discriminatory. This same directive excludes people undergoing on-the-job training, those who for some reason or other will not go on welfare or collect unemployment insurance benefits because of their pride, workers who are anxious to work and believe they can find jobs without the involvement of the commission, our young people who are being ignored, and housewives and veterans. What about the landed immigrant? In what position has he now been placed?
I have indicated by sufficient background material that I take great exception to what the minister is attempting to do. He is trying to weasle out, as it were. I hear the minister is a nice guy. We are all nice guys, but when you make a boo-boo, you must be chastised. There is no way that our feelings of friendship can affect the attitude that we on this side of the House must take.
I hope, after I sit down and other statements have been made, that the minister will say, all right, here is the directive that was issued on March 9, so that hon. members can look at it and see what it is all about.
I suggest that what the minister and the department were trying to do was wrong. They were attempting to make a very significant change in policy contrary to the UIC legislation and contrary to manpower policies. When they found that this was not acceptable the minister and the deputy minister had a tete-a-tete, and this unacceptable statement that the minister has made is the result.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the minister that it would have been better if he had not made the statement he made today. Yesterday he seemed

simply foolish. Today he appears devious. I am not sure that the combination is a wise one to show the House.
His statement was not an exercise in clarification; it was an exercise in obfuscation. I suggest, Mr. Speaker-the matter is in your hands-that as the minister referred to the statement of March 9 and then said that the new telex replaces the earlier telex it is obligatory for him, under the rules, to place the telex of March 9 on the table for all hon. members to see.
He talked in his statement today about the earlier telex having been misunderstood. If the report in the newspaper was correct, and I have not heard the minister question it, there was no misunderstanding. It was perfectly clear that the deputy minister, presumably with the minister's authority, had issued a statement that he had no right to issue, that was contrary to the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, contrary to the regulations of the Manpower Department and contrary to justice and decency to the unemployed people of Canada.

My colleagues and I agree fully that it is necessary for the Unemployment Insurance Commission to weed out the chiselers on unemployment insurance, but I condemn without qualification the way in which it is being done, hurting thousands of innocent Canadians.

speechtext:
For example, the other day the minister seemed to indicate that after the computer print-outs were available people were interviewed before they were disqualified. I want to make this categorical statement in the presence of the minister and, if I am wrong, I invite him to contradict it. There is no interview of these poor, unemployed people. They merely shove information into the computer-this is based on information that I am sure is accurate-and when they find that they are people in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits in certain categories of work and there are vacancies for those categories, the required number are sent a letter stating that they are disqualified without any personal interview. The personal interview only takes place after the person who has been declared disqualified indicates an appeal to the board of referees. I can think of nothing more unfair and more dehumanizing than this kind of treatment of thousands of people across Canada.
I say to the minister that he is doing the program a very great disservice by listing the number of people who are disqualified and giving the impression that 65 per cent of claimants are getting benefits without right when it is 65 per cent of about 10 per cent, which is only about 6 per cent. That 6 per cent will not remain 6 per cent because there may well be results after the appeals which will show that a large proportion of them are indeed entitled under the law to the benefits which they have received. The kind of zeal now being exercised by the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the minister, much too belatedly, is being exercised at the expense of thousands of Canadians who are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits and who are unemployed because of the past policies of this government. They should not be treated in the way the are now being treated.
I say to the minister that he has a duty to place the telex of March 9 on the table. He should have the courage to say to this House of Commons that he and his department made an error and that from now on they will behave in accordance with the law and in accordance with the dictates of humane treatment of unemployed people.

Mr. Speaker, according to the directive of March 9, which the minister, for reasons which we would like to know, is apparently refusing to table in this House, there would be in Canada some unemployed, young and old, educated and uneducated, males and females, who receive benefits and others who do not and finally some welfare recipients. A few unknown officials of the department decided on March 9, seemingly in collusion with the minister, to send a directive to Manpower centres asking to classify the unemployed in the order in which a job would be offered to them.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the Social Credit Party of Canada are vehemently protesting against the way the government is classifying the Canadian people as we say that all Canadians are entitled to work and the government has no right to classify them, granting to some the right to live and to others the right to die.
March 15, 1973

Manpower Placement Priorities
Mr. Speaker, today, the minister, in his statement-his telex-does not clear up the confusion which exists in the Unemployment Insurance Commission, or concerning Section 27 or the Canada Manpower Centres.
It can be seen today even more clearly that the government is embarrassed, that he does not know anymore what to do with the unemployed. And while it is playing at classifying them, interviewing them and numbering them, these people are not getting their benefits.
Mr. Speaker, the prime responsibility of the minister is not to classify the unemployed by order of priority, but rather to find work for Canadians so that each can live in freedom and security in his own country.
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Section 27, officials may classify the unemployed according to age and distinguish between people who are entitled to a job and those who are not. The minister says that he is going to consider this section and see whether it should be amended.
First, we want him to table the directive that he issued on March, 9 and to undertake forthwith to change this Section 27.
Likewise we ask that he change Section 25 of the Unemployment Insurance Regulations prohibiting a recipient from receiving benefits on the ground that he has failed to give proof that he was seeking work. One might think, Mr. Speaker, that each Canadian should submit papers, loads of them, in order to prove that he was fit to work. He says so. This is quite ridiculous and is but a pretext to refuse payment of unemployment insurance benefits.
As for us, we consider that this act should be revised by Parliament so that Canadians should not only have the right to work but that those who are unfortunate enough to become unemployed may at least benefit from a true unemployment insurance plan.
Mr. Speaker, we are disappointed at the minister's explanation today, which explains nothing since he ignored the problem caused by the improvised tax slips that do not tally with Ottawa's figures, so that the unemployed are being asked to pay tax on unemployment insurance benefits that they have not had. It seems to me that this is a most important problem, and a statement this week by the minister to clarify the situation would be most welcome.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that unemployment is still a crucial matter. The workings of the Unemployment Insurance Commission are still obscure and inefficient, while the government, instead of coming to grips with the problem, continues issuing vague orders and making life difficult for working people.
We have heard talk of a just society for Canada, for the purpose of the elections, Mr. Speaker; to our way of thinking, a just society is one in which every Canadian, regardless of race, religion or age, and whether or not he is on welfare, has the right to live in his own country, the right to fulfill himself freely in his country, and to be treated as a human being and not as a number devised by some obscure civil servant.
That is how we see the just society, and as long as the government continues to classify Canadians it will be contributing to disagreement and discontent.

Mr. Speaker, the government will have to act sooner or later.
I should like to conclude by saying that equal opportunity for all Canadians means that, instead of continuing to create confusion with his directives the minister stand up and state that henceforth there will be no priority lists of any kind in connection with the treatment of the unemployed and those on welfare, and that all Canadians, whatever their situation in life, will get the same treatment as far as the Local Initiatives Program, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Manpower Centres are concerned.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. I rise on a point of order which is based on citation 159(2) of Beauchesne's Fourth Edition. I shall read from Beauchesne, but it is word for word as it appears on page 421 of May's 18th edition:
A Minister of the Crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the House, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table. This restraint is similar to the rule of evidence in courts of law, which prevent counsel from citing documents which have not been produced in evidence. The principle is so reasonable that it has not been contested; and when the objection has been made in time, it has been generally acquiesced in.
I realize that on many an occasion members have asked for documents to be laid on the table because reference has been made to them. Your Honour, relying on the authorities, has replied that this requirement applies only when a document has been cited in the legal sense, or as would be the case in court.
I suggest that today the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) has cited the telex of March 9 in two or three ways. I might say, as one minor point, that we are supposed to believe that the new telex differs from the telex of March 9, but how can we tell unless we see the text of the telex of March 9? The minister also makes it clear in his statement that the reason for the new directive is that the original directive could be, and has been, misunderstood. Some of that misunderstanding has, of course, been here in the House itself.
Now that we have been told that there was something wrong with the original telex, with the result that it had to be replaced, I submit that we have every right to insist that the original directive be tabled so that we can make the necessary comparisons and ascertain whether this matter has been cleared up. After all, that was the purpose of the minister in making the statement he did today-to clear up the confusion that has arisen in the last couple of days. But we will not know whether the confusion has been cleared up unless we see both documents.
I submit that the requirement for the tabling of this document is based not just on the premise that the minister has referred to it or quoted from it-as a matter of fact, he did not quote-but that he has cited it in the sense of providing it as the basis for the action he has taken
March 15, 1973

today. As I say, this is clearly covered by the words in citation 159(2):
This restraint is similar to the rule of evidence in courts of law, which prevent counsel from citing documents which have not been produced in evidence.
The minister has cited the telex of March 9 as the whole basis for what he has done today, and I suggest that his having cited the document means that the Chair should rule that he is called upon to table it in the House.
I made a brief reference to the fact that the citation in Beauchesne is taken from page 421 of May's 18th edition. In that citation May has a few extra words, some of which are to the effect that the tabling must take place provided it can be done "without injury to the public interest". I certainly cannot see any injury to the public interest or injury to the state as a result of tabling the former document. Therefore, on the basis of this citation I suggest that Your Honour should advise the minister that he should now table the document known as the telex of March 9.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just have a few points remaining in my series of remarks on this bill. One of them relates to a matter which I raised yesterday, namely, the question of the economic and administrative co-ordination which does or does not exist in the Export Development Corporation and the internal development corporation which we have in this country, that part of the ministry which we call the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
Yesterday I said that it appears from the allocations of funds made by both these entities or agencies, if I may call them that, that they may be working at cross-purposes. I am glad to see from reports in the newspapers today that I am not the only one in this country who thinks that. I read in this morning's Gazette some remarks made by an official of the province of Quebec. He said and I quote:
March 15, 1973___________COMMONS DEBATES
"The only thing I can think of is that there is a rivalry between DREE and the industry, trade and commerce department in Ottawa about which one will have the key say in development plans for the country,"-
I simply repeat this point to underline what I think is an extremely important matter. It is this. We have a series of agencies in this country, whether they be ministerial, Crown corporations or what have you. that are not working together to obtain the greatest economic development of this country.
I wish to conclude my comments on this matter by referring to some remarks which were made on this topic generally by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie). I may have, not wittingly I will say, caused him to infer yesterday that I associated him rather directly with other and former Liberal cabinet ministers who had been involved very closely with Brazilian Traction, now Brascan. As far as we can tell, the minister's connection with that company is nil. At any rate, in the past he expressed views and attitudes which had been stated candidly and which should be repeated in this House. If we repeat them for the edification of this House, we are in a better position to understand what kind of presuppositions, premises and controlling principles he brings to his thinking on the matter of export development and multinational corporations. Last year he was quoted in the Financial Post as having said, and I quote:
"Multinationals are important and they produce results," ... "Do you know that in the U.S. the multinational corporations produce more jobs and more foreign earnings than the purely domestic companies? They do, and we can do the same here."
So, the minister's basic philosophy had been put on the line. It is clear. We shall know exactly what we must take into account when we deal with this legislation more specifically.
I think the minister should be reminded that when he was in charge of another ministry, the Science Council of Canada caused a report to be prepared by Mr. Arthur Cordell. The report stated very simply that Canadian-based multinational corporations were no more inclined to act in the Canadian interests than were foreign-based multinationals. This is something we would do well to keep in mind.
In closing, I should like to refer to one of the companies about which I spoke yesterday-Brascan. Brascan is informative. It tells us exactly where its interests lie. The company has produced advertisements telling us, for example, that in Canada it had assets in 1971 valued at $135 million and that in Brazil its assets were valued at $103,000,000. So, the activity of this corporation seems to be centred in Brazil. The important thing is this. We should not kid ourselves we are helping a developing country when we advance generous loans to multinational corporations, even to our own multinationals, such as the loan of $26.5 million to Brascan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, .1 do not intend to take up much of the time of the House. Most of the points have been made, and well made, and there is no need for repetition.
It does strike, me, however, that what the government is attempting to do by way of this piece of legislation is an example of philosophy they tend to adopt throughout-to use another patch in the quilt. They do not bring out any forthright long-term policy suited to the development of this country either in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce or, particularly, in the EDC. It bothers me that they should come here to present legislation before we have even seen any kind of financial statement. There is no audited statement of what they have done last year so that we can properly assess the progress being made by EDC. In other words, the government presents another hodge-podge of legislation. They show no clear evidence of developing any long-term programs, any policies. Surely, the trials and tribulations of the economy of this country are such that a new minister, particularly, should settle down and assess where we are going in this respect.
Looking at the supplementary estimates, it is obvious what goes on in this department. Throughout, there are one dollar items, indicating there has been a change of policy, modification and alternation of legislation. It is well known that what they are attempting to do is get in through the back door what they cannot get through the front door. In other words, they are trying to pass legislation by way of supplementary estimates rather than do it in the parliamentary way by bringing in bills which say what they want to do. Oh no, this is so much easier. There is that little automatic cut-off applied in the case of supplementary estimates, and debate is generally limited when considering items the department has in mind. Throughout these supplementary estimates B, we find these one dollar items thrown in, which means they really do not have a plan in the department or in the EDC to cover what is required. They put in another patch. This I deplore. Surely, a government which has been in power since 1962, throughout the last 11 years, should do better than that. They come here and ask for a little money, not taking time to present a proper bill, but dealing with one item only.
Since we are deeding with EDC, I will ask this question: how would that Corporation consider an application from a company which came to them and said "We need some money, gentlemen, to finance this project." The banker would say "Let me see the financial statement and I will consider it." "Oh no, I don't have a financial statement, just take me as I am." This is exactly what the government is asking us to do, accept them in good faith at face value. Surely, there is some business code parliament should look at when dealing with things like this. The expert Export Development Corporation comes here and asks parliament to bail them out of a situation, having overspent, having made commitments. I am reminded of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board who came to parliament seeking for an out-of-court settlement in order to avoid being sued, if the term is not too lewd, for all the

March 15, 1973
Export Development Act
money he had spent. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is the real reason for this legislation. There is no program. There is no policy. We look at what goes on within that department.
We look at Michelin Tires, for instance. The minister responsible for EDC said the other day, of course, that their only recourse was to bring a law suit in the United States if they do not get what they consider to be justice from the United States Government. I want to ask the minister in what state would the law suit be brought? Would that law suit be brought in the name of the Government of Canada or in the name of Michelin Tire? And if in the name of Michelin Tire, as it obviously must be, who would pay the court costs? This is very interesting question, and I wonder whether the minister will ever find time to reply to it. These are the types of things, this woolly, cottony attitude which this government presents to parliament every day, day after day. Surely, the people of Canada can expect a good deal more than this. And they deserve much better than this.
What has been the situation with the auto pact? We have had changing attitudes and stances, the government not knowing where they are going, or why or how. I wonder whether this is the type of government to which we are entitled. I suggest it is not.
I was under the impression-obviously mistaken-that the EDC was designed for the benefit and for the growth of Canadian industry. But as pointed out by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), loans to certain countries which would have benefitted the interests of certain Canadian industries were turned down. I wonder whether this had anything to do with the politics of Chile and whether the United States of America has still got its thumb on what this government does. Is this government afraid to act in its own right and to stand on its own feet? Certainly, its actions do not bespeak of a government with courage and foresight, one that knows where it is going.
I have said that the EDC is supposedly designed to be of benefit to Canadian industry. I notice a very curious item-I think it is item L17b in supplementary estimates B-concerning a loan to Canadair for the sale of water bombers to Spain. On the surface that is fine. If I may digress for a moment, I suggest there are too many nonlapsing loans in supplementary estimates B for this particular department. This department, with one other exception, is the only one with these non-lapsing items, these items of $1, and I suggest this is because they have no concrete policy. They know not where they go. I wish they had a light to guide their path; but there is too much heat over there and insufficient light.
With regard to this loan to Canadair to which I have just referred, it looks fine. But what was the quid pro quo that the EDC agreed to? The importation from Spain, primarily into the province of Quebec, of about $6.5 million worth of Spanish wine. I am informed that in the year 1971 the total consumption of Spanish wine in the whole of Canada was less than $2 million worth, and that the grape growers in the province of Ontario actually shipped about $1.75 million worth of wine to Quebec. Therefore, the

market for the Ontario grape grower is going to be vitally affected by this little deal.
I wonder whether there was consultation between the Export Development Corporation and the Canadian Wine Institute or the Ontario Wine and Grape Growers Association before this little deal was made, a deal supposedly for the benefit of Canada. This is what it has done for a local industry, one of the few wine producing areas of this nation. Some grandiose statements were made about saving local industry, yet with the stroke of a pen and the grant of a loan to another nation, the potential of this industry has been greatly reduced, to the point where they find it difficult to compete in Canada for a Canadian market.
Surely, it behooves this government, through this department, to formulate a plan so it knows where it is going. It should have consultations with local industry and business that might possibly be adversely affected by some of these so-called policies that the government chooses to adopt. I urge that some kind of action be taken to amend the legislation under which this particular department operates so that this non-lapsing funding is discontinued and the department does not do by supplementary estimate what it should do by legislation. Then, the people of the country will be given a clear picture of what the EDC is doing for their benefit.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising as the final Conservative speaker on Bill C-3, and I should like to sum up the arguments put forward by my party. Upon my summation, we are reluctantly willing to see this bill go to committee; but we do so on the strict understanding that we will require an intensive examination of the operations of the Export Development Corporation during this committee stage. Indeed, we may feel it necessary to suggest some amendments to the Export Development Act.
Let me sum up first. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has been guilty of shameful misrepresentation to this House. On February 2, while presenting the bill, the minister stated that the Export Development Corporation had the capacity to sign agreements for over $200 million to provide for the requirement of over $500 million. At that point the minister clearly considered signed agreements to be part of the corporation's liability under section 30 of the act that restricted such liability to $850 million, which liability restriction the minister has asked to be raised through this bill to $1.5 billion. Subsequently, however, the minister's parliamentary secretary stated on March 9 that signed agreements were not to be taken into account, although he did point out that signed agreements amounted to $865 million as of January 31, 1973. The parliamentary secretary said that it was only instruments that were to be taken into account, and that on January 31 they amounted to only $500 million.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who is right? The minister told us in February that he had only $200 million free; his parliamentary secretary in March indicated there was $350 million. The truth is that they know they are caught. There is a December 31, 1972 statement due from this corporation, and the minister is pressing to get this bill through the House because he does not want to be embar-
March 15, 1973

rassed by what that statement may show. To be more specific, the 1971 statement, in note 2, included an item as follows:
The uncommitted authority to guarantee and lend was $212 million.
If the forthcoming statement contains the same note, it would show that the uncommitted authority as at December 31 is only $9 million. Based on the parliamentary secretary's statement, therefore, they would have no uncommitted authority. Indeed, they would have exceeded it by $15 million by January 31, 1973 when the parliamentary secretary stated there were signed agreements totalling $865 million.
Let me make a prediction, Mr. Speaker. I predict that note 2, as it appeared in the 1971 statement, will not appear in the 1972 statement. They will duck the issue, and by doing so they will hope not only to duck but also to dupe this parliament. As a new member to the House, I believe it is disgraceful that the type of deception that is practised is tolerated by the House. At the very least the minister must apologize for the deception carried on by himself and his parliamentary secretary.
Let us look at how ridiculous their position is. Section 30 initially provided a ceiling of $600 million. In 1971, the ceiling was lifted to the present $850 million, because at that time it was represented that the amount committed would go over the ceiling if it was not so increased. Now, in 1973, the parliamentary secretary to the minister asks us to believe that only $500 million in notes is involved when you are determining the ceiling. If he were to be believed, why was it necessary to lift the ceiling, first of all from $600 million to $850 million back in 1971, when right now we are $100 million below what the ceiling was in the beginning, $350 million under the present ceiling and only one-third of what the government is asking for today has been committed? In other words, the corporation would be a full $1 billion under the limit they are presently asking for in order that the program can be continued. If I could effectively stop this charade I would do so, but unfortunately our right to amend this bill is limited.
Let me outline in point form the other matters affecting this bill which concern myself and my party greatly. This corporation has become the softest touch in the international financial world. It is serving in the main multinational corporations which are able to finance their operations out of the federal treasury. Out of the total capital of over $1 billion, only 43 Canadian companies benefited, and the majority are United States or foreign-controlled. In fact, over one-half a billion dollars of this financing has gone to only eight of these 43 companies.
Surely, it is ludicrous for a government to be bringing in a foreign takeover review act, while at the same time it is handing out money to the benefit of these same corporations at an interest rate of 71/8th per cent, on the average. The minister, in his rebuttal, stated that our members believe the Export Development Bank should discriminate against foreign-owned corporations, and that the job it is doing is terrible because it lends money to foreign corporations. While he admits that there could be a problem in respect of foreign ownership, he follows the usual
Export Development Act
tact of accusing our party of being anti-American or antiforeign. This is an old pattern the former hon. member of my riding used to try to discredit me when I was working within the area to unseat him. It did not work then, and I do not believe it will work now.
The people of Canada know there is a difference between discriminating against foreigners and actively encouraging Canadians. I do not believe we should discriminate against foreigners, be they American, British, German or whatever, but I do believe that we should have a government which will favour in all its actions, and through its many vehicles, including the CDC, the IDB and the EDB, Canadian-owned and controlled companies that will make their decisions based upon Canadian concerns and priorities alone. This is not the policy of the present government. It has not been its policy, and we have as yet no clear indication that it will be in the future. Surely, the Michelin fiasco should have taught this government a lesson, but that is now unlikely. Surely, the sale of that formerly all-Canadian company, which still advertises as such, Supertest, the all-British company, BP or British Petroleum, owned 50 per cent by the British government, illustrates their lack of concern.
This government's lack of concern not only for Canadian company growth but for small business is shown by what we know of this corporation's operation, and we still do not have full knowledge yet, since the accounts have not been fully audited and reported. Once again the parliamentary secretary, because of our concern for small businesses, businesses which, if given incentive and assistance, can become large, accused us of saying the corporation does not do anything at all for small business. We are not saying that it does nothing. We do say that the Canadian companies getting assistance through the EDB pay 11 per cent, while the large foreign-owned corporations pay 7 i per cent. Surely, this is a policy out of balance with our needs.
This corporation has no guidelines in respect of the amount it can lend to any single country. Surely, it would be prudent to draw up requirements that may not be violated. As it now stands, one-quarter, one-half or even a whole $1 billion could be lent to one country alone. The fact is eight countries right now have over $600 million from this corporation.
Next, I would point out that much of this financing is being utilized by these foreign countries to build transportation systems. That, in itself, is good and a valuable thing, but up to the end of December, $360 million has been pledged to such transportation systems. If our urban centres approach the federal government for funds to improve their urban transportation systems, they are told there is no money. Our priorities are wrong under the present government when a Crown corporation that is virtually out of control is allowed to dole out hundreds of millions of dollars to others, while our own people are told there are no funds available.
This corporation has many facets yet the minister, with this narrow bill, is trying to slip through only one facet of the corporation's operation without giving parliament an opportunity to look at the entire operation. If all the facts were known concerning the operation of this corporation, including its insurance of foreign investment to the extent

March 15, 1973
Export Development Act
of 150 per cent of the actual investment, it would be a national disgrace. As far as possible, we intend to bring out these facts before the committee, and we give the minister notice that we will expect him to table audited financial statements for the corporation at the committee hearings.
The government has put the gun to our head, however, in that it has indicated the passage of this bill is a priority. It certainly has top priority, because the Liberal government realized it had been embarrassed by still another bungle, having still another ceiling illegally exceeded, and by still another minister having no clear understanding with his subordinates of what constitutes fact or fiction.
The government has said it will not bring on its housing legislation until this bill has passed second reading. We do not wish to hold up whatever good there may be in the housing legislation. That, and that alone, is the reason we are submitting. What it could not achieve by persuasion, it is achieving once more by using as blackmail our known and rightful concern about the wellbeing of Canadians. We therefore will agree to allow this bill to go to the committee, but our stand in opposition to it and the tactics used by the minister in respect of this corporation is far from ended. I sincerely hope this bill will not be allowed to return to this House without significant amendment.

Mr. Speaker, the urgency of Bill C-3, to amend the Export Development Corporation Act, to raise the lending ceiling, is therefore not because the corporation has exceeded the ceiling but because its capacity to sign new agreements under the present ceiling falls considerably short of the anticipated requirements for new financing in 1973, estimated to be in the order of $500 million. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is new business for Canada, and it represents new Canadian jobs. That is the reason we have brought this bill forward at this time.
There were other references with respect to the operations of the Export Development Corporation. There was a suggestion that in some way this was a Canadian corporation which was subsidizing big business, or subsidizing the foreign-controlled multinational corporations in Canada, that in some way it was oriented to bigness and

March 15, 1973
Export Development Act
oriented to foreign control. The basic reason I think hon. members made a mistake and misjudged the situation is that they are unaware-or if they were aware they chose to overlook it, even though on occasion they were reminded by myself-that the direct loans are not made to the vendors, to the Canadian corporations. The direct loans are made to the buyers.
Let us just consider the situation for a moment. Here is a country. We will call it country X.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: No, call it Chile.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
It is a country in a different part of the world. That country is concerned with capital goods, maybe locomotives. It may be building a railway and wants locomotives. When you are looking for locomotives there are perhaps a number of countries you would consider, and perhaps a number of companies within those countries that you might consider. The Export Corporation in the United Kingdom, the ECGD, and the Ex-IM Bank in the United States, and similar types of export financing corporations in various countries would support their own industries in such a case. They would say to this country X that is looking for a supplier of locomotives, "We build good locomotives in the United States." "We build good locomotives in the United Kingdom," or in France, or wherever it is. "We would like you to buy British locomotives."
For a long time Canada was not part of this game. For a long time we let the more sophisticated export industries of the world take the cream off without Canadian initiative. But with the passage of the 1969 act, an act that was passed by the last parliament of Canada without the kind of-I don't want to use the word filibuster but at times that comes to mind-

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Come off it.

speechtext:
-by hon. members opposite, it dealt with a situation of real need. There is still a real need. Those loans are made to the buyer if he purchases Canadian locomotives. If the buyer purchases Canadian locomotives he gets a loan. If he purchases British locomotives he does not, but then he gets a loan from the British government agency to buy the locomotives. This is putting Canadian capital goods producers on a competitive basis with foreign capital goods exporters.
The EDC direct loans are oriented towards capital goods, and they are oriented to countries outside Canada. Further, they are oriented to all the businesses of Canada, because unless there is 80 per cent Canadian content there is no deal. The point which I think was often overlooked by the Conservative spokesmen is that there are literally thousands of small Canadian businesses which participate, each time one of these contracts is written.
Take the Northern Electric Company of Canada that has supplied capital equipment to countries like Turkey. It has 4,000 suppliers, and for the most part they are small suppliers. I mentioned locomotives a moment ago. Montreal Locomotive Works, I understand, adds about 20 per cent of its own content, and purchases 80 per cent from manufacturers all over Canada. In other words, these direct loans spread the benefit back, through the buyer

and the major Canadian supplier, to all corners of Canada that are involved in the manufacturing industries.
Another aspect of the EDC, that is to say, the export credit insurance aspect, is worth noting.

speechtext: That isn't before us today.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
I know that, but it was raised and referred to by hon. members, and that is why I am mentioning it in order to put the record straight. Thousands of policies have been issued under this provision. At the present time, I understand that roughly 1,000 are outstanding, and that 70 per cent of those are for amounts of less than $250,000, which is obviously an assistance to the smaller businesses in Canada. Further, they are not related just to capital goods or just to manufactured goods. They also involve consumer goods, so that this widens the application.
In committee we will have an opportunity to talk about relending loans, which is yet another aspect of the EDC's activities which brings in small business. But to suggest that through the EDC we are charging small business 10 per cent, and subsidizing big business with a 7 per cent loan, is a patent distortion of the facts.
Other questions were raised with respect to directors, the proportion of private sector directors and of public sector directors. There was a reference to the make up of the private sector directors, with the suggestion that in some way they represent only the big interests of Canada. I believe that the men who are serving from the private sector are distinguished Canadians who, in their position as directors of the EDC, are making an important contribution to the growth of Canada.
Lest there be any suggestion that there is conflict of interest, and this was raised by one of the hon. members opposite with reference to an aluminum contract, I have been informed that the President of the Aluminum Company of Canada, who is a director from the private sector, declared his interest and abstained from the vote. We can discuss whether the majority of directors should be from the private sector or from the public sector, but we are dealing with public funds and it seems to me this parliament would want to reserve unto itself the right to appoint not a majority of directors from the private sector but a majority from the servants of this parliament and this government.
Questions were raised with respect to the support of the attractive looking resort in the Caribbean. Reference was made to this as being the type of project which the EDC should not support. I am not sure it was realized that the support for this particular project was an insurance of a direct investment. There was no EDC capital used in the development of that particular resort. No resources were loaned to the developer at the other end. This was an insurance of a direct investment by a Canadian investor, and that particular part of the act is aimed at providing what might be described as political insurance, or insurance against political risk. I think it is important to note in this particular connection that that particular investment had the full support of the government concerned. In fact, the views of the government concerned were sought before the insurance was granted.

There will be an opportunity in committee to examine these questions in more detail as there will be to examine the part that the particular firms have played and the important part that these capital goods purchasers have played in terms of development of their own countries according to their own priorities. A foreign country is not going to undertake an obligation to the Export Development Corporation to repay Canada in Canadian funds for the purchase of Canadian capital goods unless it feels that the particular investment will support the development of that country according to its priorities.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I look forward to the committee stage.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
that Bill C-133, to amend the National Housing Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to begin the debate on Bill C-133 today and to move that it be referred to the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. In our discussions today, and during the debate on second reading, I want to deal with the principles of
National Housing Act
Bill C-133, an Act to amend the National Housing Act. In my view, some fundamental principles are involved in this legislation.
When we talk, as we undoubtedly will, in this debate in a general way about the subject of housing we are talking about an elemental human need-the need for shelter, for physical and emotional comfort in that shelter. When we talk about people's basic needs-the requirements for survival-society and the government obviously have an obligation to assure that these basic needs of shelter are met.
I have already acknowledged this obligation in stating that good housing at reasonable cost is a social right of every citizen of this country. As legislators, as administrators, as a federal government working with the provinces and with the private sector, that must be our objective, our obligation and our goal. The legislation which I am proposing to the House today is an expression of the government's policy, part of a broad plan, to try to make this right and this objective a reality.
The measures presented in this bill are designed, first of all, to give Canadians the kind of help that they have a right to expect in providing themselves and their families with adequate shelter. More particularly, they are directed first at those people whose need is most urgent-the old, the poor and those people who for one reason or another do not have access to the resources which this country can provide.
In considering people's need for shelter, however, we cannot concern ourselves simply with a roof and four walls. Man is a social animal and we must look beyond his house to the community of which it is a part. The community, as well as the house, must be safe and healthy and must allow and encourage man and his family to achieve the fullest possible growth and development, physically, emotionally and spiritually.
The bill is not, however, the government's only response to this challenge; it concerns only those sections which require immediate changes in the National Housing Act and it should be seen in the context of other responses which I have already described in a previous speech to the House. These are such things as the agreement at the federal-provincial conference held in January, to the development of a comprehensive national and local assessment of housing conditions. This will ensure that federal, national and regional policies are sufficiently flexible to meet the needs that exist across the country- things which are very different in different parts of the country. Such things as other parts of a total program of planned intergovernmental intervention in residential land markets-which I will mention in a moment-to reduce land costs and assist in the orderly development of urban communities; such as the growth of new intergovernment relations to assure the fullest possible consultation and co-ordination among all levels of government in developing and planning housing and community policies and programs including important changes that have been agreed upon recently for a three year commitment of funds so that federal and provincial housing agencies can plan for more than one year. As a result of the January agreement, officials of Central Mortgage and Housing are meeting with the provinces to agree upon these forward planning commitments, a part of which will

March 15, 1973
National Housing Act
be the process of getting housing away from the countercyclical economic device that it has often been in the past.
In the process of these consultations on agreement for forward budgeting, we will provide for flexibility in the allocating of funds to provinces and their provincial housing agencies to account for regional and provincial priorities and flexibility in allocating resources between the various programs of the National Housing Act.
I might mention also the thorough review which I have already announced of the federal sewage treatment program through which the federal government lends money to provinces or municipalities, their water or sewage agencies or regional governments, for the development of trunk sewers and sewage disposal plants. That program is under intensive review by an intergovernmental committee of the federal government which is consulting presently with provincial governments on their needs. I hope to have an announcement this spring on how that program will continue and in what form. An important development will entail the support of the federal government with respect to sewage treatment services. This will improve the quality of the environment and the quality of our urban life and will, in addition, be instrumental in bringing land on to the open market.
I now want to mention a bill, also on the order paper, Bill C-135, which will bring in certain amendments necessary in this field. It is known as the financial mechanisms bill and will create the federal mortgage market corporation, commonly known as a residential mortgage bank. That will provide for a liquidity of mortgage investment, which does not now exist. The bill will provide for the establishment of mortgage investment companies. I know my friends in the NDP have indicated their resistance to this legislation. I think they ought to re-examine their position on that particular bill, which is designed to make mortgage investment more attractive.

speechtext: They will never agree to that bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I hope all hon. members will examine that bill carefully and, no matter in what part of the House they sit or which party they support, that they will support it. Bill C-135, is complementary to the bill before the House.
May I mention that there is currently under wav a reorganization within Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as a result of intensive management studies within the corporation. This is being carried out to assure that the corporation, in its operations and management functions, is totally able to carry out and fulfil legislative programs that we have enacted and are enacting. So this bill before us represents only part of the total picture with respect to housing policy and with respect to meeting the housing goals of this country. In terms of legislation, this bill represents, in my view, a major attack on the housing problems that face Canadians in the 1970's. This attack will take place on a number of critical fronts. It might be well to enumerate, briefly, those ten aspects of the bill.
There is to be, first, assistance for the planning and creation of new communities where they are part of provincial plans for dealing with the problems of urban

growth-an alternative to the uncontrolled sprawl of our great cities. Second, there are to be resources to plan and finance the public acquisition of residential land, as part of an intergovernmental attack on rising land prices and as an instrument to be used for the orderly development of Canadian cities and Canadian communities. Third, there is to be assistance to low-income families who, with some help, will be able to buy their own homes rather than occupy public housing or other forms of subsidized rental housing. Fourth, there is to be increased assistance to voluntary groups such as church groups and service clubs who are willing to take the initiative in creating housing for low-income people, and particularly the elderly. Fifth, there is to be assistance to co-operative housing corporations, to encourage personal initiative in the development of housing and to offer a wider range of choice, particularly to lower-income and middle-income people, in the kind of housing they will have and the way in which they will occupy it.
Sixth, there is to be a new and imaginative program designed to preserve and improve urban residential neighbourhoods which are a vital strand in the social fabric of Canada but which may be threatened with death and decay. Seventh, there is to be a program of assistance to rescue and restore old, deteriorating housing which, with some judicious investment, could have many more years of usable life. Eighth, there will be provisions to assist Indians living on reserves to acquire existing as well as new housing. Ninth, there is to be the first step towards a full program of protection for some buyers, similar to the warranties and guarantees offered to purchasers of other consumer products. Finally, Mr. Speaker, the last feature of Bill C-133 will be new measures to encourage research and development in housing and community planning.
In recommending this legislation to the House, Mr. Speaker, I do so with the knowledge that it has been the subject of very extensive and thorough federal-provincial consultation and public examination. As hon. members know, a counterpart bill was introduced to parliament last June which had been the subject of intensive consultation with provinces. I have had the opportunity of discussing the provisions of that forerunner bill, and of this bill, in general terms with provincial ministers concerned with housing and with many municipal representatives. The most recent discussions took place at the federal-provincial conference on housing which, as I mentioned, was held here in January, of this year. The official communique of the conference expressed, after the outcome of previous consultations which had gone on at the official level was known, the general support of the provinces for these proposals.
Many of the suggestions made by provincial ministers concerned the implementation of these programs, rather than the legislative provisions themselves, and matters which are covered by regulation rather than statute. This matter will continue to be the subject of continuing consultation at the official level. It concerns not only orders in council and the regulations that support the legislation but the administrative procedures that flow from them.
As well, there has been advice and comment from many public and private organizations, and I should like to
March 15, 1973

acknowledge now my appreciation of the time and great energy which so many people have devoted to the study and analysis of these important public issues. I think all hon. members have been impressed so far with the briefs and submissions which have been tendered by interested groups of citizens who have concerned themselves with housing policy in this country. All of this advice that we have received has been carefully considered and many of their suggestions have been incorporated in the bill and will result in further changes in detail when we reach the committee stage.
I have been encouraged to find, so far as the principles of the legislation are concerned, that they have received widespread acceptance by those people and organizations who have given them careful consideration. The Canadian Council on Social Development, for example, has described the proposed programs as significant ones, which, if properly funded-and I think we should discuss funding of the programs in Committee-

speechtext: If properly funded.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: -promises to improve the accommodation of many Canadians. The Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada has written, expressing general agreement with the tenor of the amendments. The Co-operative Housing Foundation and the Ontario Habitat Foundation of Toronto joined, I understand-although not in any written form, by the B.C. central credit union which is heavily involved in housing-suggest that this bill, if passed, will represent an enormous advance over the present National Housing Act.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: What about the proposed changes?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will deal with them in a minute.
Having shown in general terms the general nature of the support for the bill, I should like to deal now with the particular aspects of the bill in terms of the principles involved and leave the discussion of the details of programs until we meet in committee, when I and my officials will discuss the bill in detail, go through it clause by clause and be examined on those clauses.
In its broadest sense, it seems to me this legislation is not only an attack on housing problems of the 1970's but is part of the government's response to the development of urban life in Canada during the rest of this century. Great cities are not and need not become disaster areas. We are all aware of the deeply satisfying aspects of life in the country and in country towns and villages. Rural areas of Canada have contributed and continue to foster some of the abiding values that have made Canada and her people great. But cities also have a contribution to make in their rich and exciting social and cultural diversity.
Our concern must be to see that Canadians continue to have a meaningful choice among places to live and work. Our irreplaceable farmland and our rural communities with their unique life styles must not be mindlessly gobbled up by sprawling suburbs. At the same time, those people who prefer an urban life must be accommodated in a way that preserves the advantages of the city while avoiding the congestion, pollution, crime and violence which have made many of the world's great urban centres almost uninhabitable.
National Housing Act
In many parts of Canada, an alternative to the continued expansion of the city is the development of new communities, either within urban-centred regions or in remote areas associated with the development of natural resources.
The new communities program, which is new to the National Housing Act, with the co-operation and participation of provincial and local governments will assist in the development of new or expanded centres offering comprehensively planned urban functions, including housing, employment, commercial and community facilities. Measures will ensure that the public retains the benefit resulting from subsequent appreciation in value of land acquired for the communities. Hon. members will note that that is provided in the bill by leasing of the public land rather than by its sale which has invariably been the practice under land assembly schemes of the past.
Very simply, then, it is my expectation that through the new communities program, which is provided for in this legislation for the first time as a federal initiative, we can make a positive contribution by taking much of the pressure off rapidly growing existing cities by creating new and self sufficient communities with the co-ordinated and rational use of existing government programs. This would take pressure off prices, the need for further farmland for development, and the need for urban sprawl and at the same time, by way of the total planning of new communities, engage in a whole series of experiments and demonstration projects using these new techniques in housing, planning and development. One such community was announced for the national capital region, south-east of Ottawa. We will be assembling the land, meeting with the regional district and over many years developing the kinds of plans we need for that community.
Associated with a new community's program is the provision in the existing National Housing Act relating to land assembly which Bill C-133 vastly improves. Land assembly has been mentioned in this House many times during the question period. The price of land is one of the most critical factors in the cost of housing in most markets throughout Canada.
All governments must be prepared to act to increase the supply of serviced land if housing is to continue to be available and financially accessible to Canadians. An over-all land strategy is necessary, and to this end I propose to encourage provincial and municipal governments to become more active in public land acquisition and servicing.
As I announced in January, the federal government is committed to at least $100 million a year for the next five years for the public assembly of land, including assistance to new communities. This figure, of course, has no reference to the vast amounts of money that have been and will continue to be spent under the existing and to be reformed trunk sewer program. Many have argued, and I have noticed this comment in the press, that $100 million per year is not enough for a concerted attack on rising land prices. It happens to be five times more than the Conservative party enunciated as their housing platform.

National Housing Act
I want to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that this amount is substantially more than any government has put forward for this purpose in the past in this country and, indeed, is substantially more than the combined requests of all the provinces in any year to date for the purpose of land assembly. I hope that the opposition, rather than concentrating on some amount, will see that the program is good. Then, we can go out and encourage municipalities and provinces to take full advantage of it and show that in actual fact that that amount is not enough. If it is not enough, we will just have to go out and get some more.
The land assembly provision is only part of the answer to the price of land, the question of land development and bringing serviced land into the market. At the federal-provincial conference, we discussed the question of land in a proposal of mine which was accepted by the provinces, namely that in this country we need a comprehensive co-ordinated land strategy directed at the question of a land policy and a housing policy.
Between the federal-provincial and municipal governments, there are four topics which have to be addressed by them as priority items. This is what I proposed at the federal-provincial conference and which was accepted. The first item is the level and allocation of federal and provincial public investment in land and services. As three levels of government, we must agree as to the level of expenditure that is required to have a concerted attack on the question of land price and land development.
The second item is the objectives and guidelines for public land banking and development. There is no sense in us simply using the taxpayer's resources and support to engage in land speculation. Purchases of land must have a purpose, namely good community planning and an effective intervention on the land market to affect the price of land in that particular market.
The third item is ways and means of co-ordinating federal-provincial and municipal activities directed toward moderating land prices on an individual market basis. If we are going to have a concerted attack on the question of land, it is going to involve all three levels of government for obvious reasons. We have got to develop more effective ways of co-ordinating activities between these three levels of government.
The fourth item is the effects of federal, provincial and municipal taxes on the price and availability of land. This is indeed a very important subject and I invited the other levels of government to address themselves on that with me. I feel that the federal commitment in this legislation, the federal commitment in terms of this budget and the federal commitment we have made to the other levels of government in wanting to develop a co-ordinated plan are in fact important features at the root of this question of land costs.
I now want to deal with a third element of Bill C-133. It is my belief that home ownership is desirable, but obviously for low and moderate income families, this is often impossible. We have to address ourselves to this problem. With some help, however, many of these low income families will be able to buy their own homes. The present bill contains provisions for this kind of assistance.

The amount of help available to a family under the assisted home ownership program is related to the family income and can be given in three ways; by reducing the interest rate on the mortgage, by extending the time over which the mortgage is to be repaid, and by a grant from the federal government to help with the monthly payments. In drafting the regulations necessary to implement this program throughout Canada, local needs and market conditions will be taken into account so that insofar as it is humanly possible, all Canadians will benefit equitably.
The aim will be, within the program regulations, to provide low income families who qualify with the assistance required to bring their monthly payments within 22 per cent of their income. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I have been concerned, as have other hon. members, about the increasing use of notices of motions for the production of papers. A very large number of motions have been put down, and in recent years the number has been growing. I have examined the responses of the government to these motions which generally have been quite good. Motions have been turned down because in some cases the papers that were requested did not exist, or there were other good reasons for turning the motions down. However, I felt, and certainly the government felt, that it would be in the interests of the House of Commons to make public the guidelines that we have now circulated to government departments, with the view that a uniform practice with respect to the production of information in the House of Commons will be developed.
I do not believe that up to the present time there has been put before the House in any form the guidelines that the government will use and which hon. members can examine as they frame their notices of motions for the production of papers. My approach and the approach of the government is exactly the approach of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Our objective is to make as much information available as possible. We believe that Members of Parliament require factual information about the operations of the government in order that they may carry out their parliamentary duties. That statement is included in the general principle. We are also aware that the desire to make available as much information as possible must be balanced against effective public administration, protection of the security of the state and rights to privacy. It is always a delicate matter of judgment to balance the desire to make information available with the effective administration of the government, security of the state and other considerations.
So on the first point, Mr. Speaker, there is no disagreement between the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself. I endorse fully the statement that was quoted, made at an earlier time by the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson). What we

have attempted to do here is to declare a general principle and then to say that there are exceptions to that general principle. While the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre expressed his displeasure with the guidelines, he did not focus on any particular one of them, nor did he give any reason why any of these guidelines should not be invoked. I hope it will be possible to make these guidelines an appendix to Hansard, so hon. members will have them available and this debate can be related to the guidelines that have been laid on the table today. I want to make a number of points with respect to these guidelines. First of all, eight of them are soundly grounded on recognized parliamentary authorities. For example, No. 1 is "Legal opinions or advice provided for the use of the government". There is ample authority to support that, and likewise guidelines Nos. 2, 7, 10, 13, 14, 15, and 16. We have not acted capriciously; we have attempted to base our conclusions upon recognized practice, and we have succeeded on relying on parliamentary authorities, both in Canada and in the United Kingdom, in establishing these guidelines.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to practices in Sweden. It is sometimes believed that Sweden has a totally open system of provision of information to the public, but the fact of the matter is that Sweden has a very wide-ranging system of exemptions regarding disclosure of public information. For example, seven of these guidelines that have been laid on the table today are in conformity with modern practices in Sweden. For example, No. 2, papers, the release of which would be detrimental to the security of the state; No. 3, papers dealing with international relations; No. 5, papers containing information, the release of which could allow or result in direct personal financial gain or loss by a person or group of persons; No. 6, papers reflecting on the personal competence or character of an individual; No. 10, papers relating to negotiations leading up to a contract, before the contract has been executed or the negotiations have been concluded; No. 11, papers that are excluded from disclosure by statute and No. 13, any proceedings before a court of justice or a judicial inquiry of any sort.
These guidelines and these exemptions are followed in Sweden which is put forward as having the recognized model, at least by some people, of the open information system. I believe when you examine the Swedish system you will find it has wide ranging grounds and reasons for refusing information, and in those areas where information is available what happens is that instead of putting this material on the record there is a much greater use of full discussion in private meetings so the information will not get on the record and, therefore, it is by that fact excluded from public disclosure. Whether we want that kind of a system in Canada is quite questionable in my judgment.
We have examined also the practice in the United States and found that nine of the guidelines which have been proposed here are in accordance with United States practice. I may refer to them just by number so that hon. members can have them available. They are Nos. 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13, 15 and 16. The purpose of that particular line of argument is to establish that the government has not

acted capriciously, but has made extensive research into practices in other countries and into other parliamentary authorities in order to bring forward a system that might be generally acceptable.
I suggest to hon. members that if they object to these guidelines they ought to object to particular items. Do they, for example, believe that legal opinions or advice provided for the use of the government should be made public? If that is their position, and we could go down through each of these guidelines, then it seems to me the opposition should take the responsibility for telling the government and the country that it believes papers reflecting on personal competence or the character of individuals in government should be made public, and that they believe government documents which include Privy Council confidences-
