The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to an article by Dr. Rowat of Carleton University. This is an interesting article which promoted the response from Professor Knight of the University of Queensland in 1966. In that interesting article there is strong defence for not disclosing internal departmental memoranda. That is one of the main areas of interest in notices of motions asking departments to produce internal memoranda.
I refer hon. members to that article and, if I may quote one or two paragraphs of some interest to this particular discussion, I will do so. I refer to the suggestion that internal departmental memoranda ought to be made public. Professor Knight said:
The civil servant may feel, too, that he must avoid placing on record anything which is likely to offend or cut across the interests of any individual or group in the community. This could affect not only the generalist administrator having a policy advisory role, but also the large body of officials whose work is concerned essentially with matters of a technical or professional nature. An officer who prepared a report on, say, the relative merits of butter and margarine, might well find himself the centre of a political controversy long before any decision about subsidies or production restrictions had been reached at the political level. Even if he wished to defend himself and had the ability as a controversialist to do so, the means open to him to do so would hardly be adequate.
In my view it is both unwise and unfair to expect civil servants to engage in public controversy; but under conditions of open access they may be forced to do so, especially since not all ministers accept the obligation to assume sole public responsibility for departmental policies and to defend permanent officials who cannot defend themselves.
Public Service
Whenever a minister did not accept the advice of his departmental officials this would be known and it would be possible for political capital to be made of it. In these circumstances ministers would surely be tempted to fill senior posts with their political sympathizers or with officials prepared always to be acquiescent. The career civil servant would thus be jeopardized and there would be a stifling of frank criticism within departments.
If officials know that what they write is to become available to the public immediately or in the near future, many will be inclined to produce public records with an eye to history. That is to say, they are likely to put into their documents only what they believe will reflect creditably on them personally or upon the administration with which they are associated.
It stands to reason that if an individual or a particular departmental official, assistant deputy minister or deputy minister was to provide confidential advice for the use of the government, then he would present that advice in a much more frank and open way than he would if he knew the advice was to be made public. That principle was stated many years ago, even though it was restated in 1966 by Professor Knight. It was stated many years ago by Disraeli who said:
The system of laying upon the table of the House reports from officers addressed to particular departments of the executive government is most objectionable. And the House ought not to insist upon the production of papers and correspondence which concerned the preparation and preliminary consideration of measures; they would thereby put a stop to that freedom of criticism which was always invited on such occasions, and which contributed so much to the perfection of public measures." If the House were to insist upon the production of such documents, "instead of the government getting what we get now, confidential reports, containing the most minute details of the opinions of officers, given frankly and freely, for the heads of departments, we shall have a system of reports framed for laying upon the table of the House of Commons, and those will be accompanied by 'confidential reports for the head of the department alone'." There have been cases in which reports of a confidential character from officers of the government have been laid upon the table of the House, to prepare the public mind and also that of Parliament, to consent to some large measure, or perhaps some considerable vote of public money; but, generally, I think it is a course which the House ought not to sanction".
Perhaps the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) would say that that is 100 years old, but it was restated recently by Professor Knight.

speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Will he tell us the value of these guidelines, particularly the one that says a cabinet document is not to be tabled, when it is left to the minister to say that one document is a cabinet document and another is not? How do we know where we stand?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
Every announcement made by a minister in the House on orders of the day, for example, or a statement on motions, issues from a cabinet decision and a cabinet document. There is no question that many of them do. But when a minister tables a statement or makes a statement, he is not producing a cabinet document. As the hon. member knows, when cabinet documents are presented by ministers to the cabinet, some of the proposals may be accepted, some rejected or the whole thing may be rejected.
What kind of a system would we have if cabinet documents were made public and a particular minister would have the world know that he was unsuccessful, for example, in having his policies accepted by his colleagues? In my opinion it would lead to the breakdown of our cabinet system. Who decides what is a cabinet document? It is not a difficult question, because cabinet documents are visible; we all know what cabinet documents are when we see them.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF BRYDEN REPORT
speechtext:
As I have said, this is a statement of policy adopted by the government, and of course it issued from cabinet and cabinet committee discussions. But all the documents that were prepared and considered have not been produced. I do not think that, as such, this is really a statement of policy by the government. If the hon. member saw the original documents, he would see them in a somewhat different form. I presume that a government could decide to make public a cabinet document if it wished, but what we are doing here is trying to establish guidelines that are generally acceptable and are sound.
Then it comes to the question of administering the guidelines. Are they properly administered? There can be difference of opinion on that score. For example, what are "papers relating to negotiations leading up to a contract until the contract has been executed or the negotiations have been concluded?" One must presume that the minister or the government is playing fair with the House if he
March 15, 1973

or it makes a refusal on the basis of guideline No. 10. One must assume that the truth is being told. If the government was not telling the truth, it would ultimately be found out. Whether it is the present government or any other government, in all these cases it would be found out.
The question really is: are these guidelines sound in principle? If we accept that they are sound in principle, the next question is: are they being administered properly? In the last few months I have taken considerable interest in this particular question because I wanted to make sure that when papers were refused they were refused on grounds that were solid in principle and that the principle was being properly applied. I have gone to various departments and ministers on occasion and asked, "Are you sure?" I think that is about the best we can do. I do not know of any other alternative.
I do not want to speak any longer, Mr. Speaker, except to suggest to hon. members that it would be useful to look at these guidelines, to consider them, to make argument about them and to determine whether they are sound in principle. If they are sound in principle, then we should attempt to administer them properly. If they are unsound in principle, then we should change them. That is why we have taken the effort to produce the guidelines and to make them available to the House. I hope this will result in a uniform practice and that hon. members will get more information rather than less. The purpose is to establish in general the principle that we give as much information as possible, with these exceptions. If this is sound in principle, it should be adhered to; if unsound, it should be abandoned. That is the gist of my argument.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first let me say that I think the House is very grateful to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) for taking the initiative in producing these regulations or criteria with respect to the production of papers.
Ever since I have been a member of this House it has been a continuous frustration to me that it has never been quite possible to know the guidelines by which notices of motions for the production of papers were either accepted or rejected, and which qualifications on occasion were enforced. Due to the shortness of notice I have not had time to examine the record on this, but I do not think it would take much effort by any hon. member to go back over the record of the past few years, look at the reasons given for tabling and for not tabling documents and to realize the sheer inconsistency with which the guidelines were enforced. I can remember one or two instances with respect to papers that where the same documents involved two departments, a motion for their release would be accepted by one department and refused by the other. One department would say that on basis of the beliefs of its officials it was not in the interest of the department to have the papers put on the record, and the other would say that according to its officials it did not see anything to prevent publication of the documents.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) has said the problem that arises far too often is not really the basic question concerning security of the state, but the basic question concerning security of the government, of individual members of it, of government departments or of departmental officials. As I say, I commend the minister for bringing this matter forward but I am a little amazed that he has gone only this far.
He has asked for comment. Considering the brief time we have had to look at this document, we can make only initial comments. If he is sincere in this matter, and I hope he is, it should not be left just for a few minutes' debate in this hour or in any subsequent private members' hour. It deserves exhaustive examination, and the place for that examination would be the appropriate committee of the House. I can think of few more important tasks that committees could undertake in this parliament than to examine the detailed nature of this document and to consider the qualifications necessary for the release of infor-

March 15, 1973
Public Service
mation in a public way. Following that, the document should be returned to this House, either in its present form or amended, for final approval.
In this way we would at least be dealing with criteria established as acceptable to hon. members of this House, and not with criteria put forward by the present government just for this period of time, to be altered without anyone's particular knowledge at a subsequent date. We have no knowledge of how long these particular criteria have been in effect. Presumably, this document is a compilation of previous regulations that have existed and it is the latest document of that type.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me again commend the minister for at least getting to this stage with this volume of criteria. As I say, the House appreciates receiving them, but this is just a first step. It is not really enough to say that these are adequate just because in other domains similar criteria are exercised with some merit.
The minister, perhaps inadvertently, gave the essential criteria that have existed for many years in terms of the tabling of papers under notices of motions for the production of papers when he said-I think I quote him correctly-that papers, in the final analysis, are not tabled either because the papers do not exist or for other good reasons. He has given us some reasons that now have been approved by cabinet and I am somewhat wondering, with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), just what papers could be tabled as a result of these criteria. As I have said, the President of the Privy Council has asked for comment. I do not want to speak at length because I do not think it would be appropriate at this time to comment on this document in detail. But let us look at the second guideline which refers to "papers, the release of which would be detrimental to the security of the state." That is an inadequate definition in terms of what might be described as security of the state. Volumes have been written on what is in fact detrimental or otherwise to the security of the state.
Guideline No. 3 suggests that "papers dealing with international relations, the release of which might be detrimental to the future conduct of Canada's foreign relations" should not be made public. I ask, detrimental according to whom? Obviously, this implies a very subjective judgment. One only has to realize the complexity and difficulty in achieving consensus on a whole variety of issues relating to foreign relations to realize that this is an impossible criterion. What the minister is really saying is that the government is free to pick and choose those documents that it feels would be harmless and not detrimental to its own security.
The same thing applies to guideline No. 4 dealing with "papers, the release of which might be detrimental to the future conduct of federal-provincial relations or the relations of provinces inter se." Again I ask, detrimental according to whom? The whole nature of federal-provin-

cial relations has been, for over 100 years, and will continue to be as long as this country exists, a very complicated, argumentative, disputative area of governmental activity and of political activity. Again, who will make the decision as to whether papers would have a detrimental effect on the future conduct of federal-provincial relations?
Consider guideline No. 7 which reads:
Papers of a voluminous character or which would require an inordinate cost or length of time to prepare.
Again, there is latitude there for a variety of positions to be taken as to length of time for preparation. Guideline No. 10 reads:
Papers relating to negotiations leading up to a contract until the contract has been executed or the negotiations have been concluded.
My goodness! The degree to which government departments are involved in continued rounds of negotiations is well known. Negotiations and contracts are not defined and the percentage of documents or of material that might be excluded from public scrutiny under this guideline is mind-boggling. Then we have guideline No. 14:
Papers that are private or confidential and not of a public or official character.
Again, we need a great deal more elaboration as to what constitutes private and confidential documents and not documents of a public or official character. Guideline No. 15 is a real whopper. If anyone has any doubt about a document being private or public, this guideline in effect provides carte blanche. It is an invitation for the government to make its own decision on each and every issue which arises, without regard to any criterion which could be enforced. It merely reads:
Internal departmental memoranda.
I submit that guideline covers a multitude of material much of which it might be in the public interest to make public. Of course, any documents that are missed under other guidelines might come under No. 16, which reads:
Papers requested, submitted or received in confidence by the government from sources outside the government.
Presumably, the person who drew up that guideline knew something about guideline No. 10 which talks about papers relating to negotiations leading up to contracts, and so on; in fact, covering all options. If the President of the Privy Council will examine these guidelines and relate them to requests for the examination of documents, I think he will find that they are unsatisfactory. It may be that he is justifying the present criteria on the basis of what some political scientists have said in recent years or what Disraeli said 100 years ago. Although I welcome the minister's adherence to the doctrines of Disraeli, I think it ought to be realized that government responsibilities are much greater now than they were in Disraeli's time. Even in the British House, responsibilities are different in the 1970s than they were 100 years ago. I was intrigued, when talking to British parliamentarians on this subject, to have my own experiences of the last few years confirmed. Indeed, when they want information or a variety of documents dealing with matters which transcend national
March 15, 1973

activities or interests, my British colleagues have to rely on an outside source, the United States Senate.
The guidelines the minister has adopted are similar to those used in Westminster. When information is not available in the British parliament, the members there may more readily obtain it from United States congressional documents which often deal with questions similar to those asked in Great Britain. I know, from reading a document as recently as this morning on the matter of defence industries, about which there has been considerable interest in recent years, that information has been made available to political scientists and others, not from their own government but from another agency, in this case the government of the United States and its agencies.
Although what the minister put forward today is useful, he missed the essential point, that put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in the latter part of his remarks. The burden of proof for not producing documents surely should be on the government. Instead of issuing these 16 qualifications or exemptions, the procedure should have been reversed. There ought to be a clear statement on when it is in the public interest to put documents on record if and when the production of papers is called for.
It has been apparent to me from the very beginning that when papers have been requested the government has avoided making clear its reasons for refusing certain documents; these reasons have never been fully explained. I think the entire reason for this debate on the production of papers is that no criteria have been agreed upon in this field, not only by members of the House but by the general public to whom we are essentially responsible.
Two things need to be done. I have already suggested the first, which is fundamental: criteria must be established. We need to establish such criteria. That matter will involve the consideration of a committee of this House. Second, there needs to be a continuing review procedure. It is not good enough, as happens now, for the parliamentary secretary to say that such and such a document is not available for this or that reason. There needs to be an effective review or appeal procedure which hon. members might use. The debates which take place to not indicate whether in the final analysis it is in the public interest to disclose documents. Therefore, I feel we need to establish such criteria.
In addition, we need to establish a review procedure. That ought to function on a continuing basis. When any conflict arises, the public ought to know clearly the grounds for refusal. The public ought to know that the refusal is not based on some subjective whim or criterion which can be used, as at present, to cover a whole multitude of sins but, rather, on certain rights. It should be known that the government was well within its rights in refusing to produce certain documents. At present there is not an appeal procedure.
In the words of former Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson, it is not only important for governments to do right; they must appear to do right. That is not the case with respect to the tabling of government documents. I suggest that the motion before the House be amended in order to facilitate the procedures I have suggested. I therefore
Public Service
move, seconded by the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldi-mand (Mr. Knowles):
That the subject matter presently before the House be referred to the Standing Committee on Privelege and Elections and, in particular, the guidelines for the production of papers tabled by the President of the Privy Council, these guidelines to be examined, with a view to accepting, rejecting or amending the same.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House turned to private members' business I was moving the second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare of Bill C-133, the government's proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. I had placed those proposals in the context of our national housing policy, our national housing strategy, and I had dealt with certain features of the legislation, namely, the new communities program, the land assembly provisions and the proposals for assisted home ownership which offer low income people a means of purchasing houses for themselves and their families rather than living as tenants in low-income housing developments.
I am not sure whether I gave an example of the way in which this would work. But as a result of federal assistance, the payments for principal, interest and taxes would be reduced to 22 per cent of the family's gross income. For example, a family four, including two children, with an income of $7,500 could receive help to purchase a modest home at a purchase price, shall we say, of $19,000. With the help available under this program, their monthly payments would be reduced to $137, compared with the $170 or more they would need to pay if they were buying their house on the open market without federal assistance.
As many hon. members are aware, most of the provinces now provide some form of assistance toward home ownership, either by way of down payment assistance, interest assistance or assistance by way of a monthly subsidy to people with low incomes who are purchasing their own homes. Federal assistance and the grants we propose making are not dependent upon the provincial programs to which I have made reference and there is no requirement that our programs be matched. The programs will, of course, work together to benefit those who
March 15, 1973

are entitled to assistance under the provincial programs as well as under the federal program. To use the words of the pension people, they will be "stacked on" to it. The two programs can mesh together in this way.
I turn now to the provisions of Bill C-133 relating to non-profit housing assistance. I think you and all hon. member will agree, Mr. Speaker, that one important agency providing low-rental housing to people has been the hundreds of non-profit housing associations formed throughout the country of volunteers who in either service clubs, church groups, union groups or veterans groups have been providing housing to low income people, particularly to senior citizens. The work done in this area has made a very valuable contribution to providing housing for those who need it. The bill now before us takes assistance to those non-profit housing associations one step further than at present.
These non-profit organizations have over the years been encouraged and assisted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as part of the senior citizens' housing policy. I say this program is important because I am aware, as I am sure all hon. members are, of the very great debt this country owes to our senior citizens in all parts of the country who have worked so hard to build Canada and who are now, in their retirement years, entitled to decent housing within their income means. In so far as the non-profit housing program eases the burden on those who have grown old, it is an important repayment of the debt which the country has acknowledged it owes to them and which we, in this legislation, also acknowledge.
I think we have acknowledged this need to assist senior citizens in many ways, not only by what we are now proposing to do by way of assistance to the non-profit housing groups to provide senior citizens, housing, but also in the other measures which were proposed in the Speech from the Throne which opened this session, as well as in the budget speech, relating to increases in senior citizens pensions, increases in the guaranteed income supplement and increases in tax exemptions which my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), has talked about.
In our desire to provide low-cost housing to senior citizens, over the past five years more than 37,000 units of housing have been built under the National Housing Act for elderly people, more than two and a half times the number of such units built in the previous 20 years. I want to put that fact on the record. I repeat that during the last five years of the life of this government more senior citizens' housing has been built under the National Housing Act than in the previous 20 years.
The present bill, Bill C-133, makes it clear that the policy of the federal government is to assist and encourage this work to the greatest possible extent. We propose in the bill to make available to these non-profit organizations, low-cost loans to the full value of the housing they propose to build or acquire and, in addition, to make them a contribution of 10 per cent of the capital cost of the project. That is to say, if a church or ethnic group or union wishes to build a senior citizens' housing develop-
National Housing Act
ment or low-cost housing development, apart from any provincial assistance that is available we will provide a mortgage at a beneficial interest rate for the full cost; and if the organization concerned needs a grant of 10 per cent to get them going, we will provide that.
Furthermore, as many members who have become involved in this program are aware, many of these organizations need money just to get started. They require funds to develop their plans to the point where they can apply for a loan, for getting architects working on the project, worrying about where and how to acquire property, how to develop a strategy for the project, and so on. In such situations we are proposing by this amendment to give up to $10,000 in what are called "start up funds" for this purpose.
In addition, these non-profit housing groups can receive the loans and grants available under the residential rehabilitation program contained in Bill C-133 and which I shall mention in a moment. That is to say, rather than a non-profit group building a new senior citizens' housing project or a new low-renteil housing project, a non-profit group can acquire older houses or older multiple unit buildings and repair them, get the repair grants that are provided under the legislation and in this way provide low-cost housing. I am going to maintain an active program of encouragement in this regard. There have been some small developments of this kind in Winnipeg, Edmonton and a few other cities, but this must be encouraged to every extent possible.
I am persuaded that giving money by way of mortgages, grants or loans to non-profit groups is not, however, the whole answer. I am very much aware of the tremendous amount of work, effort and worry that is involved for the volunteer workers in these organizations in planning and organizing low-rented housing projects, making them reality and managing them thereafter. I fully appreciate the magnitude of their contribution and I assure these groups that the skills and resources that they need will be made available within the capability of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The reorganization of CMHC which is now under way will make it much more able to respond to local needs of this kind by setting up a special group to assist them.
I should like to make one further proposal which I shall implement when the legislation is passed. There is within these public service organizations a great wealth of expertise and experience which has been dearly bought over the years in making these housing projects a reality and, among the membership, a great willingness to be helpful and to share their experience with others. I hope that when the legislation is passed and we are ready to get this program going, when the budget and the legislation have been set, we will be able to convene a national meeting of all volunteer groups involved in non-profit housing activity in order to intensify the efforts that these groups are making in providing housing, particularly, as I say, for senior citizens' groups. I think there is a need for pooling the experience and knowledge which they possess so that full advantage can be taken of these new provisions which I hope parliament will pass as expeditiously as it can.
Also related to the provisions concerning the non-profit housing association groups are the amendments relating

March 15, 1973
National Housing Act
to co-operative housing in this country. I mention that they are related because I look to the co-operative movement and to co-operative housing developments to involve themselves with the provision of housing for those of low and moderate income. Members from western Canada, where I come from, and from the Atlantic provinces who are represented in this House will be particularly aware of the part that co-operative organizations have played in the past in improving the economic condition of families both in the west and in the Atlantic provinces. In fact, in many areas of Canada co-operatives have been not just an economic instrument but part of the whole social and cultural development of the community. This is particularly true if one remembers what has come out of St. Francis Xavier University and from people who have worked there for many years. Housing co-operatives of one kind or another have a long, creditable and proud history in Canada, but for a number of reasons they have never realized, in my view, their full potential as a means of providing housing for people of low incomes.
I have sensed among co-operatives in Canada in recent years a growing awareness of the possibilities of this method of creating and owning housing, especially for the needs of people of low and moderate incomes. I feel that these organizations, which are capable of meeting the needs of many special groups of people, deserve all the encouragement that we can give them in this legislation, and the legislation is couched so as to give them that encouragement.
While assistance to co-operatives has been available in the past from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, they have not benefited from a single and concise section in the National Housing Act outlining the programs available to them. I now propose that a separate section of the act be created-as it is created by Bill C-133-in order to encourage to the maximum possible extent development of co-operative housing, to use their own words, as "a third force in the housing market". Under this section co-operatives, depending on their type of operation, will benefit from the provisions of the assisted home ownership program or the non-profit housing assistance program.
I might mention in passing that I have had an opportunity to discuss these proposals contained in Bill C-133 with representatives of co-operative organizations. As I think some hon. members are aware, they have expressed some concern about provisions regarding non-profit housing. They were concerned that references to corporations constituted-and I quote the bill-"exclusively for charitable purposes" might exclude co-operatives from assistance under this section. As a result, I will be proposing changes when the bill reaches committee stage so as to make it perfectly clear that bona fide non-profit co-operatives will in fact be eligible as charitable organizations, so they can take full advantage of these provisions.
While I am on the subject of co-operatives, I should also like to mention credit unions. In my view, they are playing an increasingly important part in the financing of housing and, as rapidly as they are able to qualify themselves-

speechtext: Why don't you join them, Ron?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I can understand my hon. friend from Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), being a land developer himself, not being much in favour of the co-operative movement. I take some credit for the passage of the first national co-operatives act this country had had for 97 years. It didn't take me that long; it took me only two years. I find some support in the fact that it only took me two years, and I take a great deal of hope from the fact that co-operatives and credit unions are playing an increasingly important part in the financing of housing in this country and should be used to the maximum extent possible to build houses for Canadians.
The credit union movement is amassing a great deal of savings through its members and is playing, as a result of these savings, an increasingly important part in financing of housing. As rapidly as they are able to qualify, we have been happy to designate them as approved lenders under the act and to extend to them benefits of the mortgage insurance fund. I strongly urge more credit unions, and particularly the central unions operating at the provincial level, to get on the bandwagon both in the interest of their membership and in the national interest to increase the flow of capital available for house building in Canada. If I may put in a plug here, the credit unions which may have some doubt as to how best to organize themselves should take advantage of the National Housing Act by getting involved in the provision of housing; they should go to my own city of Vancouver and talk to the central credit union which is one of the leaders in this regard.
My colleague, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mrs. Sauve), says that in her province of Quebec the caisses populaires are ackowledged as an important element in the collection of savings for the provision of housing. I am happy to tell my colleague that only yesterday we approved a central unit of the caisse populaire as an approved lender in that province.
I mentioned at the beginning of my speech that we were concerned not only with the building of houses and the provision of four walls; we were concerned, and must be concerned, with the nature of the communities we are building in this country. Therefore I turn now to the provisions of Bill C-133 which relate to the kind of neighbourhoods and communities we want in this country and how we as a parliament can assist in assuring that we have good neighbourhood and community planning.
I mention, first, the neighbourhood improvement program and the neighbourhood improvement provisions of Bill C-133. There are many neighbourhoods in Canada occupied by low and moderate income people where the housing is deteriorating, community facilities are lacking and the sense of community is in danger of being destroyed. The federal government believes that many of these neighbourhoods, with some financial help and some encouragement for the local residents, could be saved and could become healthy and satisfying places in which to live. At the same time, this program will have the effect of maintaining and improving existing housing-particularly for low-income people-improving the quality of the urban environment and relieving the growth pressure on the urban fringes.
March 15, 1973

Working with and through provincial governments, the federal government will provide grants and loans to improve and rebuild selected neighbourhoods, to assist in planning and acquisition of land and to create parks, recreational and community facilities such as day-care centres where they are needed. It is in the older neighbourhoods that these kind of community facilities are lacking to a very serious extent. The program will be subject to federal-provincial agreements which will spell out how the funds are to be paid out, how the residents of the neighbourhood will take part in the development and planning of the scheme and how new homes will be found for people who may be displaced because of activity arising from the program. This program is put forward in this bill as a replacement for the old urban renewal program under the National Housing Act which turned, in many cases, into a program under which bulldozers were brought in to bulldoze neighbourhoods and people out of the way. There are, surely, better ways of dealing with older areas in our cities and the neighbourhood improvement program is designed to meet that need.
Coupled with the neighbourhood improvement program is the residential rehabilitation program which is intended to be used in repairing and improving homes for people of low and moderate income. We are all aware of the unnecessary disruption and suffering that results when families are uprooted and forced to leave older homes in which they have lived for years, or perhaps generations, because these homes have deteriorated below the minimum standards of health and safety.
The moving of families and the destruction of older housing represents not only an emotional loss to the individuals involved but also an economic loss to society through the reduction of existing housing stock. I believe that considerable leverage can be gained, not to mention the avoidance of unnecessary dislocation, by allocating money to the repair of deteriorating houses and the upgrading of their plumbing, electrical and heating systems. Loans and grants are also available to landlords provided they enter an agreement to control their rents. Generally, this program will be used in conjunction with the new neighbourhood improvement program but it also can be used, as I have mentioned, for non-profit housing projects and co-operatives. Under special federal-provincial agreements it may apply outside neighbourhood improvement areas.
I mentioned that we were concerned with a program to improve the equity in our housing. The CMHC and the government of Canada over a period now close to 20 years has promoted research into housing and community planning. It has provided assistance to individuals and groups, fostered development and carried out some in-house research. There seems to be a need for the development of a program under the National Housing Act which will complement these purely research activities, motivated by active promotion and an improved program provided for under this amendment which will include experimental projects, administrative projects and pilot projects, all to improve the design of our housing and the quality of housing and neighbourhoods.
The proposed resolution, as hon. members will see upon reading it, will empower the CMHC to finance its own
National Housing Act
development activities and to enter jointly into such activities with others, as well as to accept risks associated with agreed innovative development projects undertaken by private and public groups. The corporation proposes to collaborate closely with industry and other levels of government in initiating and conducting experimental endeavours.
It is hoped that as soon as possible upon passage of the legislation, a structured series of experiments can be undertaken jointly with industry and other government agencies across the country. More specifically, because this is a new program several areas of activity are considered essential, in my view, within the scope of a development program. These would include physical projects to be initiated or undertaken either within or outside CMHC; technological developments by way of encouraging the development of new products, and efforts dedicated to improved productivity.
It is not only a physical type of thing that we need in developing new techniques. Money must be allocated and developmental projects must be initiated which concern themselves with the encouragement of the social and environmental aspects of housing by which to encourage the public to participate in the organization and the design of projects, in initiating demands upon the government and industry for new types of planning and new types of building.
To maintain and to improve the very high standard of housing in Canada there is a continuing need for a program of this type, a program of research and development. One unavoidable element of any experimental or innovative undertaking is the element of risk. Not everything you try is going to work. Experiments, no matter how well conceived and planned, which fall short of the mark, cost money and someone must be around to pick up the bills. While the private sector can be expected to shoulder a substantial part of the cost of research and development, in the public interest, should be prepared to underwrite its share of high risk innovative developments. The changes proposed through the present bill will encourage a systematic program of experimentation and will authorize Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to undertake developmental projects or share the risks of experiments undertaken by others.
There are two sections of the act with which I will deal in more detail in the committee. One relates to housing for Indians and is almost in the nature of a technical amendment. Its purpose is to assure that all the provisions of the National Housing Act are available to individuals or groups of individuals.

speechtext:
The purpose of the amendments relating to Indians is to ensure that all provisions of the NHA which give benefits to individuals or groups of individuals are available to native people whether they are living on or off a reserve; whether they are, to use the language of the Indian Act, status Indians or not. It is simply to make sure that whatever individuals receive by way of co-operative housing, low-rental housing or assisted home ownership programs, it can be obtained off the reserve as well as on the reserve.
The last feature of these amendments related to purchaser protection of homes. As hon. members know, for most families a home is the largest and most expensive single item that they will buy during the course of their working lives. Yet generally speaking home buyers do not enjoy the same kind of protection and warranties as do purchasers of less costly items such as cars or television sets. As I said in a speech a while ago, you buy a $5 or $10 steam iron and you get more warranties and guarantees than when you buy a house for the rest of your life.
You will realize, Mr. Speaker, that to me, a former minister of consumer and corporate affairs, this seems incongruous and it is a matter to which I am devoting my attention. I expect to be able to announce before many months a national system of warranties for house buyers. In the meantime, I propose amendments to the National Housing Act to deal with two aspects of this matter. Under the provisions, if accepted, if a builder goes bankrupt or becomes insolvent before completing a house which he has sold, the funds necessary for completion of the house will be advanced to the buyer through the mortgage insurance fund. The other provision is one to make sure that when the home protection development plan is announced we will have the authority of the NHA to ensure that it is implemented.

The mortgage insurance fund. The bill which we have before us and which I am moving for second reading is an indication of the concern which this government holds for the housing needs of all Canadians.
I think the provisions which I have outlined demonstrate very clearly our particular concern for the needs of low income families and represent a substantial effort to solve many of the problems which these families face. They represent a substantial advance on the present provisions and programs under the NHA. As many groups have said, we can pass legislation but if there is no funding behind it the amendments will not be very useful.
With regard to funding, the point has been made that without the necessary resources the proposed legislation will not have the desired impact in solving Canada's housing and community problems. I would like to point out that during the past five years the federal government has been responsible for the provision of sufficient funds to construct more than 170,000 units of social housing-more than two and a half times as much as was produced in the previous 20 years.
We have allocated-I will obviously want to discuss this matter in the committee when we get there-for the first year of operation an amount which we think realistically can be spent under those provisions, considering that

many of these programs will be in the start-up stage. If the provinces, municipalities and industry were able to use up the funds which I will be proposing for this fiscal year once the legislation is passed, further amounts could be transferred from other programs to meet the need. So far as I am concerned, the first job is to get the legislation passed and then to ensure that sufficient funds are available to carry out in an effective way the program which the legislation provides. I will be very happy when we reach the committee stage of this bill to discuss budget figures with members of the committee. I have tried, in accordance with the rules, to confine myself today to the principles of the bill but I will discuss in committee the budget matters.
As I mentioned at the outset of my remarks, this legislation is a key element in the government's over-all thrust to meet the legitimate expectations of all Canadians to be well housed in healthy and satisfying communities, whether they be in the country, villages, towns or the great metropolitan centres. This bill provides some of the legislative instruments to achieve this goal. They will be backed up by all the dollars that are needed to get the job done. I will close my remarks by repeating what hon. members have heard me say many times before, namely, that these measures deserve and require the support and participation of all governments in Canada and of people everywhere who have ideas, energy and enthusiasm to bring to the task of providing housing at reasonable cost to all Canadians.
In moving second reading, I hope we will have a constructive and useful debate on Bill C-133 and that it can be expeditiously moved to the committee where we can start to deal in detail with the provisions of the legislation, because CMHC, the government and those in the country who want to provide housing cannot deal with any of these proposals until they are passed by parliament and given royal assent.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the minister for an hour and 15 minutes paint such a beautiful picture of urban affairs and of the housing situation in Canada, I cannot help reminding him of a Latin expression, caveat emptor-let the buyer beware. In this case he was the salesman selling a package to the Canadian people, and the Canadian people should beware the package that was sold them. I am reminded that in one of the most famous stories by Dickens, "The Cricket on the Hearth", it was said that four walls and a ceiling never made a home. I suppose, Mr. Speaker, the most important thing today is to get four walls and a ceiling into such a position that the average Canadian can afford them.
The first problem, as I see Bill C-133 and the statement which the minister made on Monday, March 12, as recorded at page 2095 of Hansard, together with his contribution to the throne speech debate, is that all the changes made since the passage of the National Housing Act in the first instance have been made on an ad hoc basis. The minister admitted in his opening remarks that he had part of his plan in Bill C-133. He also had a plan when he spoke in the throne speech debate, and he had a plan last Monday as set out on page 2095 of Hansard. He is trying to remedy the housing situation and improve the quality of life for Canadians on an ad hoc basis.
When we come to grips with the general philosophy, the first questions we must ask ourselves is, what kind of housing policy do we really want in Canada? Where are we going with that policy? Will we get there on an ad hoc basis? What should be the objective of a housing program acceptable to our national urban development? In a nutshell, the objective of any national housing policy, within the terms of the constitution of Canada, should be an attempt of the government to plan, to adopt and to create a program whereby during their lifetime every Canadian family should be able to afford a house wherein they can gradually build up an equity, with an area of grass around the house and the kind of environment which provides a good quality of life, so that some day they can achieve either ownership or a substantial equity which would be an incentive to own a house. It may be that people will start out in apartments or town houses, as it were, and
25789-71*
National Housing Act
end up with such an equity ownership in a house, or vice versa.
Every Canadian is entitled to a home with a landscape. This should be the national thrust. This should be the national purpose of housing. This should be the urban jurisprudence of any housing project. I must say, as I read the bill, that on an ad hoc basis it falls far short of that kind of philosophy guaranteeing Canadians that during their lives they will have substantial equity in a home in which they can raise their families. I was hoping to hear that kind of philosophy from the minister.
Although the bill before the House has many good amendments to the National Housing Act and is great for propaganda purposes and for talking points, it falls short of achieving any real, long-term, long-time planned project for housing in order to improve the quality of life in our larger urban centres such as Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg and other cities. If we start now at this stage in our history, we can prevent the failures, the frustrations, the ghettos and the absolute poverty that have become part of the cities of the United States and of many European and Asian countries which I have seen, which you have seen, Mr. Speaker, and of which the members of this House are aware. Canada, a young country and a new country, full of resources, can do better.
Hence, first, the main objective is to put within the pocketbook of every Canadian the right to build up an equity in a house, where a family lives in a house with a little landscape, like a touch of wilderness, in peace, happiness and dignity, where the beauty of life is magnificent, rather than in an environment where the germs of crime breed on ignorance and illiteracy, without enlightenment to lead to the goal of a way of life to build a vigorous, strong and intelligent people and, therefore, a healthy nation.
A new national policy for housing cannot be brought about by a band-aid bill, and I call this a band-aid bill. The minister has admitted that it is a band-aid bill. He says, "Well, I have got some of my policy in this bill. I have some of my policy in the other bill. I have some of the policy that I set out in the Speech from the Throne debate, and some of my policy that I set out the other day on motions." It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that on that last day I was in Alberta at a political meeting, but when I read his announcement as reported at page 2095 of Hansard, I found it strange that the same kind of policy was announced in the province of Ontario. What he really did on that occasion was to promote a provincial program.
I say that this is a band-aid bill prepared on an ad hoc basis. The band-aid method will for a short time help to cure the wound; certainly it will help ease the housing crisis but in the final analysis the wound will become more infected for the crisis will remain within and will deepen until a sociological problem will develop, a revolutionary tendency will mature and violence and unrest will fester in our midst.
We will support this bill going to committee. But the facts of the bill must be laid naked in the hope that out of the committee's study there will be created, for the first time since World War II, a national housing development policy, an integral part of a national urban affairs policy

March 15, 1973
National Housing Act
which will solve the crisis, a crisis that I will deal with in a few moments, that of housing and all the problems facing people in urban centres.
What kind of crisis am I talking about, Mr. Speaker? It has become, and continues to be, the major tragedy everywhere. A new national development and urban affairs policy with emphasis on housing, rapid transportation and the quality of life is the only answer. I should like to read again from the Toronto Star which I quoted when I was questioning the minister in the House some time ago. To relieve the conscience of my friends across the way, I will also read from the Globe and Mail. As my friend says, it will even it up. The article in the Toronto Star reads in part:
Major social tragedy. Less than 4 per cent of Toronto wage earners can afford a new home says a study by the urban development institute-
Not any newspaper, not politicians, parliamentarians nor legislators, Mr. Speaker.
-which calls the city's housing situation a major social tragedy.
Listening to the Minister, I would not have thought him a lawyer from Vancouver but, rather, a house salesman trying to sell a few houses to a few Canadians. This is the whole tragedy, Mr. Speaker. Think of it-only 4 per cent of the wage earners of a major city like Toronto can afford a new house! That has been the policy-if it is a policy-of this decadent Trudeau government.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The article continues:
The study, released Wednesday, warns that "unless drastic action is taken immediately, this situation will become more desperate."
The institute's figures are based on a comparison of 1961 and 1971 incomes.
In 1961, a $5,284 annual wage was needed to buy a house, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation reported. In 1971, an income of $16,623 was needed to buy a house and only 4 per cent of the population could afford it.
Only that kind of income can afford a new house under the plan which the minister has outlined tonight. Then we find these words in the article:
The institute, which includes developers, builders and architects, blames a shortage of land for the skyrocketing prices.
"Lot prices around Toronto are now the highest on the continent," the report states.
Toronto is one of the fastest growing cities on the continent. The article goes on to say that average lot prices in Toronto are about $18,000 and the cheapest house today in the city of Toronto, one of the major centres of the country, is $35,000. That is under the housing plan outlined tonight on the ad hoc basis of the bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Get your facts straight.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My friend says I should get the facts straight. I say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that he should write to the Urban Development Institute and not to me. This is a statement made by the institute. If my friend wants to listen, let him listen. If he does not, let him go back to his constituency and they will tell him about housing. The article goes on to say:

To ease the situation, the study urged the provincial government to redirect funds for major sewer and water services.
The tragedy I am talking about is summed up in that manner. Time does not permit me to deal with the whole picture. The common ground for most of the grievances is contained in the report of the task force on housing, headed at one time by a minister of the Liberal government who now sits over here, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), except that the delay in the implementation of the recommendations contained in that report has deepened the crisis. They should be working for the good of all Canadians now, but instead the report has been gathering dust for the last three years.
Let us come to grips with the problem. Two problems must be solved immediately in the area of housing and urban affairs. The first problem is money and the second is the price of serviced land; to get enough money into projects and reduce the price of serviced land. Larger sums of money must be made available for an effective national housing policy to improve the standard of life and urban standards such as a rapid, non-polluting transit system, parks for leisure and rest, and sufficient and adequate playgrounds for our youth. These must be part of a national development program for urban affairs and for housing.
I suggest that the first problem is money, Mr. Speaker. If this government can afford, by its bumbling, a $2 billion program for unemployment insurance to assist the unemployed-it did not solve unemployment; the problem was aggravated by their policies-it must be prepared to share more money with the provinces and municipalities than $100 million for land bank costs. In a few moments I will read from the Globe and Mail to show that when the minister embraced his great land bank program under which he is pouring out $100 million a year, the immediate response from one large city was to apply for $93 million. Mr. Speaker, that would only leave $7 million for all the other cities in Canada. When dealing with land banks, the most important thing is to get serviced land ready for development, rather than raw land. The $100 million will not last long, considering the high cost of serviced land.
I have dealt with Toronto, but it doesn't matter which city you deal with: the minister's home city of Vancouver, the cities of Calgary, Edmonton or Winnipeg or Halifax- the facts are the same. Let us see how far this $100 million will go in the land bank. The Globe and Mail of January 29 wrote:
The province's land bank is the assembly it is now carrying out south of the proposed Pickering airport site. Coupled with the original federal government announcement of the airport were plans for provincial assembly of 25,000 acres. In December, Queen's Park applied to Ottawa for a CMHC loan of $93 million to cover 75 per cent of the estimated cost of the land assembly.
Toronto needs $93 million, and the minister says he has solved the problem of the nation. He says that by setting up $100 million for a land bank he has solved the problem. That is raw land, Mr. Speaker, not serviced land. If this amount were granted to Toronto it would leave only $7 million available to the other cities to solve their problems. We could afford $2 billion for unemployment insurance to help the unemployed. That unemployment was brought about by the policies of this government to cure inflation, and they still could not do it. Before the election
March 15, 1973

the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was asked about this in Edmonton and he said if the Canadian people did not like it, they could lump it.
If we can afford that kind of luxury, $2 billion, surely the minister, with all his salesmanship and his public relations officers, could make a better deal than offering the Canadian people $100 million for a land bank to solve the problems of the cities. Toronto needs $93 million, and you have only to look at the map to see who owns the land around Toronto and what the situation is there. My friend says the Tories own it. One thing I would say, through you, Mr. Speaker-when it comes to getting into the hog trough, the Liberals have never been backward. A report in the Globe and Mail of January 9, 1973, reads:
Though news reports at the time made little of this announcement, $93 million is almost as much as the total amount the federal government has lent for public land assembly projects across Canada since the program was set up-
I received a letter the other day from a man who has knowledge of the housing situation. Speaking about Scarborough, he said that adjacent to Toronto vacant land sells for a price ranging from $40,000 per acre to $65,000 per acre. He mentioned parcels for a single family, detached dwelling units, services being available, although planning and interior services are not complete. When we talk about land, we mean land ready for development, that is, serviced land. It costs approximately $30,000 to service an acre of land today. If the land costs $65,000 and servicing it costs $30,000, the total cost is $95,000. If the regulations in the area concerned say that you may only subdivide at the rate of four lots per acre, the cheapest lot today, March 5, 1973, is $23,750. Yet the minister, who comes from Vancouver where there are grave difficulties, said today that this bill will solve the problems of people in Canada. That is why I say, let the buyer beware.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Caveat emptor.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, let the buyer beware. The cost of land is one thing; the cost of serviced land is another. Any land, whether held by a public land bank or by private developers, must be brought into use quickly if it is to be of benefit; that is, it must be serviced quickly. There is no sign in the bill that there is to be federal leadership given to provinces or municipalities in creating serviced land. The point is this. Although the minister may purchase $93 million worth of land in Toronto, that is not serviced land. On top of that cost there is $30,000 an acre to be considered for putting in services. Therein lies the problem. Nothing in this bill suggests that private enterprise or land banks owned by the government will meet the difficulty. No inducement is held out for development and for bringing land into service quickly. The first thing the federal government must do is to provide leadership in this field.
What is the purpose of a land bank? A land bank in itself may be good, of course. If a high quality of leadership is provided, land may be serviced and brought into use for housing. On the other hand, if you buy land today and wait only three or four years, the land will increase in
National Housing Act
price; consequently, the extra cost will be passed on to the house purchaser.
The minister talked about land banking and how fine it was, but those were merely high-sounding, beautiful phrases. What a salesman the minister is. He is superb. I have sat in the gallery watching Members of Parliament and I say the minister is a superb salesman. He taiKed about land banking and the $100 million that will provide big solutions. Those were beautiful, high-sounding phrases. I invite him, with the committee, to go to our cities.
Let me talk about my own city. It is always said that Calgary is affluent. Let us begin with my constituency, Calgary North, where in the last two or three years public housing has been built which can best be described as ghettos. Workmanship is poor and the materials have just been thrown together on the land. These projects were expensive. However, asking families to live in them is like asking them to live in ghettos that are worse than those of the United States or Europe.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Has the hon. member complained to the carpenters?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.

Mr. Speaker, I assure the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) that we like his help. It adds colour to the debate. I hope other hon. members over there see the light.
First, tri-level conferences should be set up on an agenda basis and not on an ad hoc basis. The federal government must bring the municipalities together and propose a tri-level conference which understands the needs of the people. The needs vary from area to area. From my reading of the bill, and I hope I read it accurately, the needs of various regions will not be considered. What is good in Newfoundland and would help the people there may not apply to the people in Toronto or Montreal, and what may be good in Montreal or Toronto may not meet the needs of people in western Canada. Therefore, we need a flexible policy. That kind of policy can only be created if we create the kind of national housing program that is flexible, that will meet the needs of Canadians in all areas. That would be fulfilling the spirit of confederation.
The minister mentioned the meeting involving the municipalities. After that meeting was over I received letters telling me that, certainly, the provinces met with the federal government and with the minister, but the mayors of municipalities were just decoration at that meeting. We on this side of the House asked if we could attend that conference to see what was going on. We learned that the representatives of municipalities performed about as much function at that meeting as window-drapes in an office building. Is it not wonderful how the minister spread his arms and said, "What a policy we evolved and what a meeting we had when we got together." I wish to quote what a Vancouver alderman said:
Last week, I was in Toronto for the first meeting of the three levels of government in the history of Canada. It was an important meeting for the municipalities because it gave them some recognition as a legitimate third level of government, but it was a disap-

pointment in that there was no commitment to any long term tri-level consultation.
The first thing the municipalities should do is get their tri-level conference on an agenda basis. The mayors of our cities should have some say. The city of Montreal has a larger population than most provinces. The city of Toronto is larger in population than any province except the one in which it is situated, and the province of Quebec. Surely the mayors, aldermen and experts of our large urban centres should be able to talk, irrespective of the constitution, on the same level as the minister because they represent thousands of people, and in some cases millions.

When we had the great tax reform bill it was painted as a great reformer. Now the government has to have Fred Davis sell the public. It is to do as little as possible, and if you are ever asked to do anything which looks difficult, blame the constitution. Loans for services are good in themselves but direct grants should be considered. Federal loans to cities increase the over-all debt of those cities, preventing them from obtaining credit by way of debentures.
I just want to spend a few moments on that thought. In the program the minister announced tonight he spoke of loans with respect to sewage disposal plants because large ciyes were still pouring raw sewage into the rivers. The reason they will not come for the loans is very simple, and I wish the minister would get closer to local government. As soon as the federal government lends a province or a city money for that sort of thing, their liabilities are increased and when they go to get credit ratings to get debentures they are turned down. speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING NEIGHBOURHOOD IMPROVEMENT, REHABILITATION, OWNERSHIP, NEW COMMUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to say a few words now about specific projects, although my colleagues on the committee will be dealing directly with many of these points. Public housing is a "must" today because there are so many people in Canada below the poverty line. Why has this system been brought about? I think if we could have a

March 15, 1973
National Housing Act
system which did not demand public housing we would be a greater and better nation. I referred a while ago to the jurisprudence of the national housing policy I should like to see for Canadians. Surely that is the kind of system under which every person could own a house or have an equity in a house. But today they have to get into public housing. I say its a "must" because the low income groups have tried for years, but cannot afford housing either by way of equity or rent. As I see it, the only way we can solve that problem is to bring up the income of those people and also ensure that the purchasing power of a dollar is there. This This will improve the financial capacity of people so they are able to afford something better than public housing.
I have received dozens of letters, since I was asked to take on this position, from people all over Canada complaining about public housing. Really, what they are saying to me is that public housing, the way it is being administered today, will become the ghettos of tomorrow. And that is my warning. Public housing is good in itself, but public housing not properly administered, with proper care, proper supervision, with pride of equity and pride of ownership, is only beginning the seeds of new ghettos for Canada. Yet people talk about public housing as if it is a newborn baby with all the qualities and a high IQ.
Co-operation housing is good if it creates a right of equity and the qualification to obtain mortgages. This will be discussed by other members of my party. One hundred per cent mortgages: I am for it provided they are not used by house developers or anyone else for the extra profit of 10 per cent. What do I mean by that? Over the years in this country we have had 8 per cent loans and 9 per cent loans. What really happens? They get the land together and the mix goes on. They put the property together and they finally come out with a profit of 80 per cent to 90 per cent. So a hundred per cent mortgage really means another 10 per cent going somewhere else. It is not going to help the ordinary person.
I have always felt that as Canadians we should differentiate ourselves. We are a new country; that is why people from Europe and Asia came here. Surely in a new country the ambition of every red-blooded Canadian is to walk into a house some day, lay down the payment on that house and say, "Some day I will own it". What inspiration is there when you give a man a 50 or a 60-year mortgage? He has to take good care of his health if he is ever going to have title to the house.
A lot has been said by the minister about rehabilitation. The days of the bulldozer, I am glad to say, are over. They were started by this government. Knock down everything that is in your way. Cost-sharing between the federal government and the provincial government is good, but as I read the act the federal government says: In our generous way we are going to give $2,000, and that $2,000 will be matched either by the municipality or by the provincial government. Four thousand dollars! There is an open end to the bill, to be fair to the minister. Governments other than the federal government can put in more dough. Assume they do not. Generally, it is dollar for dollar. Go into the cities where there are run-down houses. Start hiring the plumbers. Start hiring the carpenters. Start

buying the materials. Four thousand dollars is not enough to renovate the average roof, let alone the house. It sounds beautiful when you put it in words, but when you explore it in practice it is just like a hungry elephant eating a peanut.

Again, money is the number one solution. If we are to have a new national urban development program as outlined by me on behalf of my party, this cannot be achieved by a department of government which is directly independent of the government. I am not being critical of CMHC. Over the years they have done a great job. They have had some great presidents. But surely when we ask the government, from this side, to set up an urban affairs department and they finally concede and put the minister where he is today, one of the things they should have done was to make CMHC responsible to that department of the government. As I see the corporation, it is as independent as the CBC or the Bank of Canada. The minister could have the finest program in the world, but if that independent agency slowed it down to a crawl, the minister's program would be slowed down to a crawl.
So the recommendation I would make tonight is that in some way CMHC be made directly responsible to the minister so that the minister can give us direct answers to our questions when we ask about the actions of the corporation. I do not intend to go into the mechanics of how this could be arranged, but the draftsmen could certainly work something out. When we asked him about rent increases affecting old age pensioners, he said it was according to some contract. The next day he said it was according to some dividend program. He said he had issued a directive. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what the agency can do? We heard a lot about directives today. They can throw it into the wastepaper basket. So why not adopt a more realistic approach? Let us make CMHC responsible to the minister so that it is really a part of his department like any other department of government.
Therefore, there needs to be a new amendment to the National Housing Act, or an act setting up a department of urban affairs and making the minister secretary of state for urban affairs and housing, so that, as with any other department of government, he set the tone of policies and the department carried them out. The minister would be responsible for the department's administration, its successes, its errors, its adversities and its achievements. The last, of course, would be somewhat difficult. If a deadlock or disagreement occurred between the present setup of CHMC and the minister, outside of the good will that they have today-and which I assume all ministers have-without any legal thrust or implications, the minister could not implement his policy.

CMHC is more independent than the CBC and the Bank of Canada and many other crown corporations. speechtext:
That is right, they will only take so much. The time is fast coming, if we are going to work with all levels of government so as to have that degree of control within the terms of the constitution, when the federal government will be able to give leadership not only in developing new communities but in improving old communities. They must work, as I said, under a new national urban development policy and a new national housing development policy, so that pollution control can be effective, so that money-wise, rapid transit systems can be implemented, not only in newly developing areas but in established areas, and so that the whole quality of life in the city can be improved and men and women and their families can live in proper accommodation with dignity and happiness. This policy could become the greatest tool in halting the increase in crime. For crime breeds in poverty and poverty exists in ghettos. The growth and development of youth in the nation is only a product of the environment from whence they spring.
I am almost finished, Mr. Speaker, but when dealing with differences between what happens in Newfoundland, what happens in Ontario, what happens in Alberta and what happens in British Columbia, perhaps a small poem written by Don Harron in satirical fashion might do a lot to show what I mean by differences between people. It is entitled, "Ode on You, O Canada" and it is from the book "Charlie Farquharson's Histry of Canada". My son gave me this to read, and when I read it last night I felt it added the right touch. I have not ended on a poetical note for some time, so if the House will forgive me I should like to put it on the record. I am sure I will get the ears of the House because I do not put this forward in a partisan way. I rather like it:
What is Canada to you?
This land so strong and true.
Have you ever before heard the words "This land so strong and true", Mr. Speaker?
What does it make you think of,
And why and where and how?
Whenever I think of my country,
It seems like a great big cow.
Yes, a Guernsey or a Holsteen,
Is that sich a foolish notion?
Lappin' its fill of the waters Of our very own Pasifick Ocean.
Then chewin' its cud on the Prayerees,
Right over yer Kickin' Horse Pass In the breadbasket of our nation,
As it regurgitates its grass.
And settles its mash in Ontaryo,
National Housing Act
Then to the loins of our country,
Where somethin' surely is stirrin'!
Listen and you can hear
A rumblin' and grumblin' and whirrin'.
The wind of change is Mowin'!
Can't you hear its howls?
As we wonder at all those movements
Deep in our nation's bowels.
And so we come to the end of my tail
And all its little rimes . ..
And doesn't this alius happen
To the dear old Marrytimes?
